title: BMW's new iX4 is almost here, with 428 miles of range and seriously fast charging
content:
Peter Johnson
| Nov 23 2026 - 7:21 am PT
new iX4 is almost here, and it could make range anxiety a thing of the past. With 428 miles of EPA range, more than 500 miles on the WLTP cycle, and ultra-fast charging, the new EV could make road trips a whole lot easier.
BMW iX4 enters production ahead of March 2027 launch
Series production of the new iX4 is officially underway at BMW Group’s manufacturing plant in Debrecen, Hungary.
The iX4 is the second fully electric BMW model built at the facility, following the
record-breaking production ramp-up
of the new iX3 SUV.
BMW said the plant began series production of an entirely new model in less than two months after the company introduced a 24-hour, three-shift schedule to ramp up output to meet higher-than-expected demand.
will go on sale in March 2027 as an all-electric replacement for the X4. It will be available in two variants: the BMW iX4 50 xDrive and BMW iX4 40 xDrive, with a range-topping M60 xDrive set to follow shortly after.
Both versions use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The iX4 50 xDrive provides a combined 468 hp and 475 lb-ft of torque, enabling it to sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 4.7 seconds.
BMW launches series production of the new iX4 (Source: BMW)
The performance M60 version delivers a combined 603 hp and 645 lb-ft of torque, which BMW says is good for a 0 to 60 mph sprint in just 3.9 seconds.
The iX4 features a distinct coupe-SUV-like silhouette rather than the traditional boxy, upright SUV design of the iX3. With a rakish roofline and an aerodynamic design, the new iX4 has a drag coefficient of just 0.23.
Like the iX3, the iX4 is based on BMW’s Neue Klasse architecture with its sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive system.
BMW iX4 M60 (left) and 50 xDrive (right) (Source: BMW)
While EPA figures have yet to be finalized, BMW said the new iX4 has an estimated driving range of up to 428 miles on a single charge using a 112.2 kWh battery. Under WLTP conditions, it offers an all-electric range of up to 514 miles (828 km).
Thanks to its 800V architecture, BMW’s new iX4 can add up to 184 miles of range (384 km on the WLTP cycle) in just 10 minutes with charging speeds of up to 400 kW. Charging the vehicle from 10% to 80% takes about 21 minutes.
BMW iX4 interior (Source: BMW)
Like BMW’s other Neue Klasse models, the new iX4 features its updated interior design. The setup includes a large 17.9″ infotainment screen and BMW’s new Panoramic Vision, a 42″ display spanning the base of the windshield.
The iX4 is 188.3″ long, 74.6″ wide, and 63.3″ tall, with a 114.1″ wheelbase, which is about the same size as the iX3. However, it’s slightly lower than the iX3 thanks to the sloped roofline.
Like all Gen6 BMW models, the new iX4 supports bidirectional charging, enabling it to be used as a mobile power source for e-bikes, camping equipment, or other electrical devices.
BMW iX4 50 xDrive
will go on sale in March 2027, starting at $66,300, or $4,800 more than the iX3 50 xDrive. That doesn’t include the $1,495 destination fee.
In Germany, the new BMW iX4 40 xDrive starts at €70,900 ($77,500), and in the UK it’s priced from £53,250 ($69,500), OTR.

title: If you can't beat 'em: VW to export 300,000 Chinese-built cars per year by 2030
content:
Volkswagen
manufacturing
Jo Borrás
| Nov 23 2026 - 4:39 am PT
With declining sales, annual capacity cuts approaching a million units, and a wave of affordable Chinese competitors entering Western markets, Volkswagen is facing down its own mortality. Rather than fighting it, the company is leaning in and announcing plans to export roughly 300,000 Made-in-China VWs per year by 2030.
American dealers won’t be getting any Made-in-China vehicles (not at first, anyway), but for Mexican, South American, Middle Eastern, African, and Southeast Asian markets, the shift to lower-cost Chinese manufacturing marks a major strategic pivot. In addition to exporting budget-friendly sedans like the Jetta VA3,
Volkswagen is also considering a move to adopt Xpeng’s tech stack for up to 75% of its core European lineup
Does Volkswagen have any other options?
Jetta SUV concept; by FAW-Volkswagen.
The move comes as Volkswagen’s Chinese JVs face a sharp sales decline in their home market, selling just 1.2 million new cars in the first nine months of 2026 (down 35% compared to last year). The financial story is even worse, with last year’s roughly $815 million profit falling to a more than $120 million loss.
“The sharp decline in the overall market in China remains an industry-wide challenge,” said Martin Sander, Volkswagen Group’s sales boss, before adding that VW’s “new,
locally developed electric models are beginning to make an impact
Add in rising energy costs
, continuing software issues,
and serious labor disputes with the IG Metall union in Europe
, and Volkswagen may not have much choice in the matter – which is why it’s not exactly surprising to see VW consider turning China into an export hub. And that 300,000 number? That may be just the start.
On Volkswagen’s third-quarter results call, CFO Arno Antlitz reportedly called that 300,000 annual export target “conservative,” adding that overseas shipments could help offset the carmaker’s weakening prospects in China.
Here’s hoping those export plans eventually expand to the US. After years of pushing upmarket,
seeing a reborn electric Jetta on US lots would feel like a true return to Volkswagen’s affordable and accessible
“people’s car” roots.

content:
Markets & Policy
Lebanon is working towards adding at least 3 GW of electricity generation capacity in the coming years, most of which is expected to come from solar and wind, alongside battery energy storage.
Patrick Jowett
23 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Lebanon’s Cabinet of Ministers has approved a plan to increase the country’s electricity generation capacity by at least 3 GW to 3.5 GW over the coming years, including a focus on deploying solar, wind and battery storage installations.
The plan was presented by the country’s Energy and Water Minister Joe Sadeh during a cabinet meeting last week.
According to a statement published by the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, Lebanese citizens currently face high energy costs and rely heavily on private generators, while national utility Électricité du Liban struggles with high operating costs and grid outages.
The newly-approved plan will see natural gas-fired power plants continue to provide baseload generation, with the government agreeing to import liquefied natural gas to supply existing power plants. It also acknowledges solar, wind and storage projects as a key way to increase generation capacity in the coming years, while committing to enhancing and rehabilitating existing hydroelectric power facilities.
The government is also exploring cooperation with Qatar to accelerate the development of new renewable energy and storage projects.
The ministerial statement says potential cooperation could involve government-to-government arrangements with private sector participation under a design-build-operate-transfer model.
Ministers also discussed investment in Lebanon’s electricity transmission network to accommodate additional generation capacity and reduce existing bottlenecks.
The government statement says work is underway to involve the private sector in distribution and collection, through distribution system operators, according to the framework adopted by the Electricity Regulatory Authority. It explains the model would split the country into geographical and technical operating zones, with performance monitored by the authority.
“This operator is responsible for reducing technical and non-technical losses and increasing collection rates, according to clear performance indicators monitored by the regulatory authority,” the statement continues. “Ownership of the network’s assets remains with the state.”
Lebanon’s cumulative solar capacity stood at 1,505 MW by the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), up from 1,081 MW at the end of 2024.
In September, the country introduced
new permitting and safety rules for PV systems
up to 1.5 MW, including the establishment of municipal oversight and technical requirements for installations.

title: Wind-driven spray system cools, cleans solar panels - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers have developed a water spray system that cools and cleans PV modules using a wind turbine coupled directly to a mechanical pump. In rooftop tests, the system lowered cell temperature by up to 26.7 C and increased peak power output by 18.6%.
Lior Kahana
23 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
A research team from Iran has designed and investigated a novel self-cooling and self-cleaning system for PV modules. The system is wind-driven, using a vertical-axis wind turbine, which drives a mechanical water pump via a belt. The pump feeds a nozzle that sprays water onto the module surface to cool it and wash away dust.
“First, the system introduces a direct mechanical conversion of wind energy into pump operation. By eliminating generators, batteries, inverters, and grid connections, the proposed system operates with zero electrical power consumption,” the team said. “This fundamental design shift eliminates parasitic pumping losses, ensuring that 100 percent of the PV-generated electrical output is preserved and utilized.”
The researchers built the vertical-axis wind turbine from two second-hand bicycle rims, a connecting rod, and a support frame. They made the blades by cutting 110 mm PVC pipes lengthwise into half-pipe sections, each 70 cm long, and sealing the ends. A belt transferred rotation from the turbine shaft to a mechanical pump, which drew water from a reservoir and sent it through a hose to a nozzle directed at the front surface of the PV module. The pump began operating at about 1 m/s and could continue running at lower speeds once started.
The team tested the system on a rooftop in Farrokhshahr, Iran, using two identical 60 W polycrystalline PV modules measuring approximately 70 cm × 70 cm each. One module received the spray, while the other served as the control. During the May-June field campaign, the researchers monitored module temperature, voltage, and current between 7 a.m. and 6 p.m. They recorded wind speed and solar irradiance every 10 minutes and logged ambient temperature and water volume hourly.
“The thermal results demonstrated that the wind-driven spray system significantly reduced the cell temperature, with a maximum temperature difference of 26.7 C between the conventional and cooled panels, corresponding to approximately 36–37% reduction during peak radiation hours,” the results said. “The daily temperature behavior indicated that the cooling effect was most pronounced during midday under high irradiance and moderate-to- high wind speeds, while in early morning and late afternoon hours, the temperature difference decreased by >76% due to lower solar radiation.”
The results show that the cooled panel generated higher output power throughout the day, with maximum power increasing from 50.1 W to 59.42 W, an 18.6% improvement. Even under low-irradiance conditions, power increased by up to 25%, indicating stable system performance. The average daily energy efficiency increased from 10.37% to 11.47%, a 10.6% improvement directly attributed to reduced thermal losses.
“Economic analysis showed that despite a <2% increase in initial and maintenance costs, key financial indicators improved substantially: net present value (NPV) increased by approximately 29%, internal rate of return (IRR) by 12.6%, and levelized cost of energy (LCOE) decreased by 11.4%, confirming the cost-effectiveness of the proposed system,” the academic group concluded. “The payback period and energy payback time decreased by approximately 10% and 9.9%, respectively.”
The research, “
Experimental investigation and multi-dimensional analysis of an integrated wind-powered spray cooling and cleaning mechanism for PV panels
,” appeared in
Results in Engineering
. Scientists from Iran’s Shahid Chamran University of Ahvaz and the Technical and Vocational University (TVU) have contributed to the study.

title: Europe turns negative electricity prices into a flexibility signal - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Negative wholesale power prices are a useful investment signal for batteries and demand response in Europe only where subsidy design and grid bottlenecks are not distorting them, says a new Eurelectric report.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
23 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
Negative electricity prices do not necessarily indicate a failure of European power markets. They can direct investment toward energy storage, demand-side flexibility, and electrification when they reflect actual supply and demand conditions rather than regulatory distortions or structural barriers.
This is one of the main conclusions of “
Negative prices in EU power markets
,” a new report prepared by economic consultancy Compass Lexecon for European power industry association Eurelectric.
The analysis examines negative prices across European wholesale electricity markets and distinguishes between episodes that provide economic signals for adapting the power system and those associated with contractual incentives that influence generation bids.
When negative prices reflect genuine economic conditions, they can support flexible resources. When they persist because of infrastructure constraints or poorly designed support mechanisms, they can create inefficiencies and additional costs.
Negative prices
The report identifies significant differences in the frequency and duration of negative prices across European electricity markets, reflecting variations in renewable penetration, storage deployment, and the technical and regulatory characteristics of each system.
Spain and the Netherlands recorded negative electricity prices during approximately 7% of the hours in 2025. Following a widespread increase between 2015 and 2024, some countries subsequently experienced stabilization or a decline, while others maintained an upward trend.
Renewable generation growth alone does not explain these differences. Demand-side flexibility, grid constraints, battery availability, and generation-related incentives also influence the frequency and severity of negative prices.
The report highlights Finland as an example of how electricity systems can adapt to economic signals. Negative prices occurred during 8.3% of the hours in 2024, falling to 5.3% in 2025. During the first half of 2026, their frequency stood at approximately 1%.
Eurelectric links this development to progress in electrification and battery energy storage, which have increased the system’s ability to absorb electricity during periods of high availability.
However, the study warns that price signals alone may not stimulate investment when regulatory barriers or infrastructure limitations remain.
Some generation support contracts, particularly earlier schemes, can encourage facilities to continue producing during negative-price periods to avoid losing support payments.
These incentives can lead generators to submit bids below their actual variable costs, deepening negative prices and distorting signals for other market participants. Poorly designed mechanisms can also result in inefficient dispatch and additional costs for consumers.
The analysis examines different contract for difference (CfD) configurations, including arrangements that suspend support payments during certain negative-price periods and mechanisms that decouple support from actual electricity output. Hybrid designs are also considered.
These alternatives differ in investment risk allocation, dispatch efficiency, and implementation complexity. Existing contracts present an additional challenge because their duration can prolong incentives contributing to structurally negative prices. Options include adapting certain agreements where appropriate and subject to corresponding compensation arrangements.
Storage investment
Negative prices can strengthen the economic opportunities available to battery storage and demand response, supporting investment in resources capable of adapting electricity markets to higher renewable penetration.
However, grid access barriers, infrastructure limitations, and revenue uncertainty can prevent price signals from translating into additional flexible capacity.
The report assesses long-term flexibility procurement mechanisms as one option to improve revenue predictability and direct investment toward specific system needs. These mechanisms must be designed carefully to avoid distorting competition with assets operating without contractual support in balancing and ancillary services markets.
The study also identifies greater participation by industrial and commercial consumers, aggregation of distributed resources, and electricity contracts combining price stability with incentives to adjust consumption as potential sources of flexibility.
The report’s findings come as EU member states work on national flexibility needs assessments (FNAs).
According to estimates from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (Entso-E) cited by Compass Lexecon, European electricity system flexibility needs could double by 2033, driven by renewable generation growth, electrification, and changing consumption patterns.
The study argues that these assessments should identify which flexibility needs can be met through market-driven investment and which might require additional procurement mechanisms. They should also distinguish structural limitations from temporary imbalances to avoid public measures compensating for distortions elsewhere in the regulatory framework.
Compass Lexecon identifies three areas for action: limiting distortive incentives in support mechanisms, removing barriers to flexible resource participation, and using additional procurement instruments where market-driven investment is insufficient.

title: Jordan plans 200 MW solar, 100 MW/400 MWh storage projects - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Investor prequalification for the solar project is expected to open in February 2027, followed by prequalification for the battery storage project a month later.
Patrick Jowett
23 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Jordan’s Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources unveiled plans for new large-scale solar and storage projects during the inaugural Jordan-EU Investment Conference, held last week.
The ministry is planning to invite private investors to develop a 200 MW solar project and a 100 MW/400 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in the new year.
Both projects will follow a build-own-operate model, with state-owned National Electric Power Company purchasing the electricity generated by the solar project and acting as the beneficiary of the storage project.
The solar project is expected to require an estimated $100 million to $130 million in investment. Initial requests for investor prequalifications are expected to be issued in February 2027.
The 100 MW/400 MWh BESS is expected to require an investment between $70 million and $90 million. An initial request for investor prequalification is expected in March 2027.
Further details, including the planned locations of the projects, are yet to be announced.
The two projects form part of a wider investment package also including plans to develop a 100 MW wind project, a 450 MW pumped-storage hydropower project, shared infrastructure for green hydrogen and green ammonia production and natural gas infrastructure projects.
According to the Jordan News Agency, the projects form part of Jordan’s efforts to attract international investment, expand private sector participation in energy infrastructure and strengthen energy security, while supporting the country’s transition towards cleaner energy sources.
Jordan’s cumulative solar capacity stood at 2,195 MW by the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), the same figure reported at the end of the year prior.
In September, the country’s energy regulator approved the
first 200 renewable energy systems
under its revised regulatory framework, which allows consumers to access several arrangements depending on their customer category and consumption profile.

title: Hydrogen shifts summer solar to winter in Japanese apartment building - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Japanese contractor Takenaka has run a hydrogen system that stores surplus summer solar power for winter use in an apartment block in central Japan for a full year and says it worked as planned, though it has published no performance data.
Brian Publicover
23 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Green Hydrogen
Hydrogen
Japanese construction company Takenaka Corp. said its hydrogen-linked energy management system at a 24-unit apartment building in Kurobe, Japan’s Toyama prefecture, has moved surplus summer solar power into the winter months as intended during its first year of operation.
The system pairs I.SEM, an energy management system Takenaka developed to integrate distributed power sources such as solar arrays, batteries, and electric vehicles, with a power-to-gas hydrogen system.
Surplus solar electricity in summer is used to produce green hydrogen, which is stored in a hydrogen-absorbing alloy and converted back into electricity and heat by a fuel cell in winter, when solar output is lower. Waste heat from hydrogen storage and the fuel cell supports the building’s central hot-water supply, which runs on heat pump water heaters, according to the company’s release.
The system is installed in Building O of the fifth block of Passive Town, a housing development by YKK Real Estate in Kurobe. The seven-story building, completed in March 2025, has 2,387 m2 of floor space.
Takenaka said a one-year evaluation of the system, which started operating in April 2025, confirmed that hydrogen produced in summer was stored and later used to generate electricity in winter, and that the battery and other distributed resources were managed as planned. The company aims to supply 95% of electricity demand in the apartments themselves, excluding common areas, from on-site renewable energy alone.
The Osaka-based contractor described the project as the first installation in Japan of a hydrogen-utilizing energy management system in an apartment building.
The company did not disclose the capacity of the solar array, battery, electrolyzer, hydrogen storage, or fuel cell. Nor did it publish how much hydrogen was produced, how much electricity the fuel cell generated, or the share of demand met by on-site renewables in the first year. It said it will continue to monitor the system’s operation.
Japanese contractor Taisei Corp. has tested a similar approach for seasonal storage at a
zero energy building test facility in Yokohama
, using two 450 kWh lithium-ion batteries, a 5.0 Nm3/h proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer, a 2,000 Nm3 hydrogen tank, and a 5 kW fuel cell.
Other building-scale solar-to-hydrogen projects in Japan include a
solar-powered hydrogen production trial at a high-rise office complex in Tokyo
, whose backers also have not disclosed system capacities, and a 2023 pilot by Sekisui House-W that uses
surplus rooftop solar to run a small electrolyzer in a residential building
. Economic curtailment of solar has now occurred in every transmission system operator area in Japan, after
reaching the Tokyo area in March 2026
Researchers from Finland’s LUT University and Germany’s Regensburg University of Applied Sciences have identified
high investment costs and the low efficiency of converting electricity to hydrogen and back
as major drawbacks for seasonal hydrogen storage in residential solar systems.

content:
Markets & Policy
Saudi Arabia’s updated framework sets out new connection requirements, fees and net billing rules for renewable energy systems installed for self-consumption.
Patrick Jowett
23 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Saudi Arabia
The state-owned Saudi Electricity Regulatory Authority (SERA) has updated its rules for renewable energy generation facilities designed for self-consumption.
The regulation covers renewable power systems, including solar, wind, waste-to-energy and biofuel installations, at homes and other buildings that are designed to meet consumers’ electricity needs. It stipulates that generation and consumption must take place at the same facility and permits integrated battery storage systems.
A statement published by the Saudi Press Agency says the new rules aim to improve installation, connection and operation procedures while clarifying requirements for consumers, enhancing safety and efficiency, and protecting consumer rights.
The updated regulation raises the maximum generation system capacity covered by the framework from 2 MW to 50 MW. Grid-connected systems are now divided into four categories: 1 to 11 kW, above 11 kW to 50 kW, above 50 kW to 2 MW, and above 2 MW to 50 MW.
Systems in the first category, typically residential-scale installations, require no prior approval before installation but must be notified to the service provider and installed by an accredited contractor. There is no connection fee for this category.
The second category, covering systems above 11 kW to 50 kW, requires an accredited contractor and a feasibility study and is subject to an application or connection fee of SAR 700 ($186.95). Systems above 50 kW to 2 MW require an accredited consultant or contractor, as well as a network impact assessment, and are subject to a SAR 2,300 fee.
Systems in the final category, above 2 MW to 50 MW, require a study permit and a generation license from SERA. The application or connection fee is set at SAR 16,500 for systems between 2 MW and 4 MW, increasing to SAR 35,000 for systems above 4 MW.
The regulation requires service providers to process connection requests in the order they are submitted via an electronic platform. Providers are also required to publish a list of qualified contractors and approved equipment, as well as details of available network capacity.
The regulation also sets out a framework for mandatory net billing, under which surplus electricity exported to the grid is credited financially.
Credits are carried forward to the next billing cycle, where they can be deducted from electricity charges. The framework says credits can be used across multiple accounts, provided the accounts belong to the same consumer, and are valid for 12 months from accrual.
SERA’s updated framework comes three years after it first issued regulations for renewable energy self-consumption. It also consolidates two existing regulatory frameworks for renewable energy self-consumption and small solar energy systems.
Saudi Arabia installed around
of solar last year, taking cumulative capacity to around 12.4 GW.

政策分类路径: 政策 > 监管落实型政策 > 市场势力 > 公平信息接入 > 纠纷解决与监管机制
政策分类依据: 法案允许能源项目开发商就差别待遇起诉监管机构，并缩短司法挑战时限，属于争议解决与监管机制
content:
Markets & Policy
The US Senate has approved a federal permitting overhaul that would shorten court challenges to energy projects and let developers of solar, wind, and other energy projects seek damages from agencies over a pattern of disparate treatment, in a Nov. 19 vote that sends the bill to the House.
Brian Publicover
23 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
The US Senate voted 62-33 last week to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), a bill that would overhaul how US federal agencies permit energy projects, transmission lines, and other infrastructure, and open a route for developers to sue agencies over alleged disparate treatment of their project types.
The Senate passed the bill as an amendment to H.R. 2347, a tax bill the House of Representatives had already passed, after agreeing on Nov. 18 by 69-27 to replace that bill’s text with BAAJA. The House must now act on the Senate amendment before the bill can go to the president. BAAJA was
introduced in the Senate on Sept. 30
Under Section 1402 of the Senate-passed text, sponsors of 46 listed project types, including solar, onshore wind, and storage as well as fossil fuel, nuclear, and transmission projects, could sue over a permit denied in bad faith or delayed more than 60 days past a deadline as part of a pattern of disparate treatment, according to a section-by-section summary by the Bipartisan Policy Center (BPC), a Washington-based think tank. Plaintiffs would need statistical evidence comparing their treatment against the previous 10 years, and damages would range from 50% to 100% of a project’s reasonably expected construction cost.
Section 1401 would bar agencies from revoking, suspending, or materially amending a permit in effect on or after Nov. 6, 2026, subject to six exceptions, including court orders, material breaches, fraud, and urgent harm, according to BPC. Where bad-faith interference is proven, sponsors could recover 25% to 50% of development and construction costs from the federal Judgment Fund, which pays court judgments against the US government.
The bill would also cut the deadline to challenge projects under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the US law requiring environmental reviews of federal actions, from six years to 150 days, according to BPC. Courts that found a NEPA violation could only send the decision back to the agency without voiding the permit or halting the project, and the agency would have no more than 180 days to correct it, it said.
Grid provisions
The bill’s transmission title would require the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to issue permits for qualifying lines, including those of 230 kV or more and projects in approved regional plans, once a state has had one year to act, according to BPC. Reconductoring, voltage upgrades, added circuits, advanced technologies, and energy storage within existing rights-of-way, the land already secured for power lines, would be exempt from NEPA and historic-preservation review.
The bill would also allow behind-the-meter resources, including batteries installed on the customer side of the utility meter, to be aggregated into wholesale electricity markets within 18 months, and would give FERC 90 days to revise its policy so data centers pay their share of grid costs plus incremental costs, said BPC.
The Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) praised the four sponsors after the vote. The US trade body said its analysis shows the bill could unlock 167 GW of additional solar capacity between 2028 and 2035, raising solar’s share of US electricity generation to more than 18% by 2035.
The Sierra Club opposed the bill as it moved toward a vote. Ahead of the Nov. 9 procedural vote, Executive Director Loren Blackford said the legislation remained deeply flawed despite improvements made in a manager’s amendment, and called for an open amendment process. In an Oct. 8 analysis of the bill as introduced, the environmental group listed “Eliminating the power of the Courts to act on legal violations” among its concerns.
The bill must clear the House before the current Congress ends in early January, when a
newly elected Democratic majority takes office
, or it would have to be reintroduced. Earlier this month, Wood Mackenzie described BAAJA as the
primary vehicle for accelerating utility-scale solar, battery storage, and high-voltage transmission
after the midterm elections.
The Senate vote comes as US solar and wind developers contend with Interior Department rules, introduced in July 2025, that subject projects on federal land to
elevated review by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum
. SEIA has opposed the rules and
warned of rising consumer costs from federal permitting delays
. On April 21, 2026, US District Judge Denise J. Casper in Massachusetts
issued a preliminary injunction against the Interior policy
, finding that challengers were likely to succeed in showing it was arbitrary and capricious under US administrative law.

title: Daikin launches R32 retrofit solution for existing residential heat pump series - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Japanese manufacturer claims its retrofit approach can reduce installation time by up to 22%, capital expenditure by up to 55%, and energy consumption by up to 16%. The new range comes in three capacity classes and incorporates integrated refrigerant safety technology.
Emiliano Bellini
23 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
Daikin Mini VRV 5 S-series outdoor unit
has introduced new replacement technology for its R-32 (difluoromethane)-based Mini VRV 5 S-series heat pumps, enabling existing variable refrigerant volume (VRV) and variable refrigerant flow (VRF) systems using R-410A refrigerant to be upgraded to R-32 equipment while retaining suitable existing refrigerant piping and wiring.
According to Daikin, installation time can be shortened by up to 22% and capital expenditure reduced by up to 55% compared with a complete system replacement. The company also claims energy savings of up to 16% compared with equivalent R-410A systems.
The new Mini VRV 5 RXYSA-B replacement range will be available in three sizes – 4 HP, 5 HP, and 6 HP – and uses R-32 refrigerant, which has a global warming potential (GWP) of 675, approximately 68% lower than that of R-410A.
The existing Mini VRV 5 S-series platform offers nominal cooling capacities ranging from 12.1 kW to 15.5 kW and rated heating capacities of 8.4 kW to 10.7 kW, depending on the model. Maximum heating capacities reach 18 kW under specified test conditions.
The outdoor units feature a compact, single-fan design with a height of 869 mm, low-noise operation down to 39 dB(A), and support for total piping lengths of up to 300 meters.
The technical specifications refer to the existing RXYSA-A platform, as detailed performance data for the newly introduced RXYSA-B replacement models have not yet been confirmed.
The systems also incorporate Daikin’s Shîrudo refrigerant safety technology, designed to facilitate the use of mildly flammable R-32 refrigerant in occupied buildings. It includes integrated refrigerant leak detection sensors, audible and visual alarms, and automatic shut-off valves to limit refrigerant leakage.
According to Daikin, the factory-integrated safety measures facilitate compliance with IEC 60335-2-40 and simplify system design and installation, particularly in smaller indoor spaces.

title: REK 2.1: Humanoid robots show off kicks, falls, and blade clashes
content: Humanoid robots have entered the combat sports arena, with a Silicon Valley event showcasing machines exchanging punches and kicks.The event, held on November 20, called REK 2.1, brought together human-shaped robots for physical bouts in front of a live audience in San Francisco.The matches highlighted how advances in robotics are enabling machines to perform increasingly dynamic movements, including striking, recovering from falls, and engaging opponents. In September, an EngineAI T800 humanoid, developed in China, fought in San Francisco at REK’s first human-versus-robot event.Humanoids trade blowsHumanoid robots have taken their fighting abilities into the entertainment arena, exchanging punches, kicks, and even blade strikes in a series of combat matches in San Francisco. The demonstrations took place at REK 2.1, an event organized by Robot Entertainment Kombat (REK), which brought four humanoid robots together for three matches before an audience of about 200 people.The matches featured several humanoid robots with distinctive designs and appearances. One of the contestants was T-Rek, a robot standing approximately 180 centimeters (5.9 feet) tall, with a silver skull-like face and red eyes. Its opponent, Radar-72, featured a helmet and a brown-and-sand-colored camouflage pattern across its body.The two machines traded punches and kicks, both trying to recover quickly after being knocked to the ground. During their approximately 90-second bout, T-Rek landed a kick that left Radar-72 unable to get back up. The defeated robot was subsequently carried out of the ring on a stretcher, reports Chosun.Other contestants included Bad Boy, which featured a purple helmet with horns and green lights, and Lectile, a black-bodied humanoid with decorations resembling dreadlocks.The final match introduced another level of physical combat, with the participating robots equipped with three blades on each hand. The machines engaged in sword-fighting movements, producing metallic clashing sounds as their weapons struck each other.The robots also attempted more complex movements, including flying kicks and attacks against opponents lying on the ground. Their repeated collisions with the arena’s transparent protective panels produced loud impacts, while scratches, chipped paint, and small pieces of debris appeared during the matches.These demonstrations showcased the mechanical capabilities needed to move rapidly, maintain balance, and recover from falls during physical interactions. Unlike conventional industrial robots designed for repetitive tasks, the humanoids were configured for dynamic movements in an unpredictable combat environment.Operators control the fightingDespite the use of AI, the robots were not independently deciding how to attack or defend themselves. Human operators positioned beside the arena controlled the machines using game console-like controllers.Operators determined the robots’ movements, attack directions, defensive actions, and when to execute punches or kicks. AI-assisted systems helped the machines execute those commands while maintaining balance and controlling posture.This arrangement allows the robots to perform physically demanding movements without requiring every aspect of their balance and motion to be manually controlled. However, the demonstrations did not establish that the machines could independently plan and execute complete fighting sequences.The event also reflected the growing interest in humanoid robotics among technology workers and the wider public. Spectators watched the matches through protective panels, recording the fights and cheering for their preferred robots.According to experts, the increasing use of humanoids in physical competitions also presents new engineering and safety challenges. Robots equipped with blades or capable of delivering powerful kicks could pose risks if their movements become unpredictable or their control systems fail.The event highlighted questions surrounding the strength of protective barriers, permissible weapons, attack power, and emergency shutdown procedures. These concerns have become particularly relevant following earlier attempts to organize human-versus-robot combat events.REK previously held a September 18 match in San Francisco featuring influencer Frankie Lapenna against humanoid robots. On September 23, the California State Athletic Commission issued a notice ordering the organizers to stop unpermitted human-humanoid combat events.

title: J-20 Stealth Fighter's Radar Signature could nearly double with 10% coating loss
content: A new study by Chinese researchers suggests that damage to the radar-absorbing coating on the J-20 stealth fighter could significantly increase its radar signature. Laboratory measurements indicate that losing just 10 percent of the coating could nearly double the amount of microwave energy reflected under certain experimental conditions. The findings highlight how even relatively small areas of peeling or damaged material could weaken an aircraft’s ability to suppress radar reflections. The research also underscores the maintenance challenges involved in preserving the stealth capabilities of advanced military aircraft.Radar signature doublesChinese researchers have found that losing just 10 percent of a radar-absorbing coating could nearly double the amount of microwave energy reflected by a material, highlighting how relatively small areas of damage can weaken stealth technology.The findings offer insights into a maintenance challenge facing advanced stealth aircraft, including China’s J-20 and the US Air Force’s F-22 Raptor. Although the researchers did not test either fighter’s proprietary coating, their laboratory experiments demonstrate how different forms of surface damage can affect a material’s ability to suppress radar reflections, reports the South China Morning Post (SCMP). The researchers investigated how scratches, surface wear, and complete coating detachment affected microwave absorption. They prepared a composite material using carbonyl iron powder, a magnetic microwave absorber, and silicone resin, which provides heat resistance and environmental stability.The composite was sprayed onto titanium alloy plates to create a coating 1 millimeter (0.04 inches) thick. The researchers then introduced different types of damage, varying the affected area, depth and location. They measured microwave reflections across frequencies ranging from 2 to 18 gigahertz.The experiments showed that the impact on radar-absorbing performance depended heavily on the nature and extent of the damage. In one test, removing 10 percent of the coating increased the minimum reflection level from minus 12.73 decibels (dB) to minus 9.78 dB. This 2.95 dB difference represented an approximately 1.97-fold increase in reflected microwave power.Peeling weakens stealthScratches had a relatively limited effect, even when they covered 50 percent of the sample’s surface, because most of the absorbing material remained intact. Similarly, mild surface wear caused limited deterioration when it affected no more than 20 percent of the surface and penetrated up to 0.4 millimeters into the coating.More extensive wear produced a stronger effect. When damage covered 50 percent of the surface and penetrated 0.6 millimeters into the coating, the minimum reflection level increased to minus 7.37 dB. The researchers attributed this deterioration to changes in coating thickness that disrupted the electromagnetic matching conditions required to minimize reflected waves.Complete detachment proved particularly damaging because it exposed the underlying titanium alloy. In an experiment involving central detachment, removing half the coating increased the minimum reflection level to minus 2.91 dB, compared with minus 9.12 dB when only 10 percent was removed.The location and shape of the damage also influenced performance. Central and strip-shaped areas of detachment had a greater impact than damage near the edges of the sample. According to the researchers, exposed metal reflects electromagnetic waves strongly. The boundaries between the remaining coating and exposed substrate also create discontinuities that generate additional diffraction and scattering, further weakening the material’s ability to suppress radar reflections.The findings highlight why maintaining the integrity of radar-absorbing materials is important for stealth aircraft. Earlier reports have identified coating deterioration and repair requirements as challenges for the F-22, while Chinese researchers continue to investigate more durable radar-absorbing materials. However, the study does not establish how the tested composite compares with the operational coatings used on either fighter.

title: Scientists' new 3D printing breakthrough could transform titanium alloy design
content: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have developed an innovative titanium alloy design strategy that could pave the way for stronger, more durable materials for aerospace, automotive, biomedical and other advanced engineering applications.Led by Prof. ZHANG Tianlong, Assistant Professor in HKUST’s Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, the research team has introduced a novel approach based on three-dimensional (3D) compositional waves enabled by additive manufacturing. The technique uses in-situ alloying during laser powder bed fusion, a metal 3D-printing process, to create interconnected, microscale variations in molybdenum (Mo) concentration within the widely used Ti-6Al-4V titanium alloy.Titanium alloys are used for their high strength-to-weight ratioThe research, titled “Compositional architecting by additive manufacturing enables hardenable titanium alloys,” was recently published in the prestigious journal Nature Communications.Titanium alloys are valued across several industries for their high strength-to-weight ratio, excellent corrosion resistance and, in biomedical applications, strong biocompatibility. Despite these advantages, conventional titanium alloys generally have limited strain-hardening capabilities.Strain hardening allows a material to become stronger as it undergoes plastic deformation. When this capability is insufficient, deformation tends to concentrate in specific regions, a phenomenon known as strain localization. This can compromise a material’s ability to withstand further loading and limit its reliability in safety-critical applications.HKUST team explored a fundamentally different approach to alloy designTo address this challenge, the HKUST team explored a fundamentally different approach to alloy design. Instead of pursuing a chemically uniform composition, they deliberately introduced spatial variations in alloying elements to control how different parts of the material respond to mechanical stress.Using additive manufacturing, the researchers created interconnected 3D compositional waves of molybdenum within the Ti-6Al-4V alloy, producing three distinct regions with different phase stabilities and deformation characteristics.Each region contributes a different deformation mechanism when the material is subjected to mechanical loading.Low-molybdenum regions contain cooling-induced α’ martensite and deform through detwinning and retwinning. Medium-molybdenum regions contain a metastable β phase, which progressively transforms into martensite under applied stress. Meanwhile, high-molybdenum regions feature a stable β phase and primarily deform through dislocation slip.Mechanisms work togetherCrucially, these mechanisms work together rather than independently. Their interactions generate heterogeneous-deformation-induced (HDI) stresses, allowing different deformation mechanisms to become active progressively as the applied stress increases.This sequential and cooperative response helps maintain strain hardening over a wider range of deformation, delaying strain localization and improving the alloy’s ability to withstand mechanical loading.The resulting Ti64-6Mo alloy demonstrated impressive mechanical properties, highlighting the potential of this new design strategy.The material achieved a strain-hardening increment of approximately 557 MPa, more than twice the typical upper limit reported for conventional titanium alloys. It also recorded a tensile strength of 1,236 MPa and a uniform elongation of 11.5%.These results demonstrate that carefully engineered compositional variations can improve the combination of strength and deformation resistance, offering a promising route towards titanium alloys with enhanced mechanical performance.Challenging the traditional approachThe study challenges the traditional approach to alloy development, which has largely emphasized achieving homogeneous chemical compositions throughout a material.Instead, the HKUST research demonstrates that chemical heterogeneity can be a valuable design feature. By controlling the spatial distribution of alloying elements, researchers can tailor phase stability and coordinate multiple deformation mechanisms within a single material.Commenting on the significance of the findings, Prof. Zhang said, “This study shows that alloy design does not have to focus solely on the overall uniform chemical composition. By controlling how alloying elements are distributed in three-dimensional space, we can coordinate multiple deformation mechanisms within a single material. Compositional architecting opens up an extra degree of freedom for designing the next generation of high-performance structural alloys.”The concept of compositional architecting could have implications beyond titanium alloys. Its potential extension to other advanced structural materials may open new opportunities for developing materials with tailored mechanical properties for demanding engineering applications.By combining additive manufacturing with three-dimensional compositional control, the HKUST team has demonstrated a new direction in materials engineering—one in which the strategic arrangement of chemical elements becomes as important as the overall composition in determining material performance.

title: Could a new planet be hiding at the edge of our solar system
content: Astronomers may be one step closer to solving one of the biggest mysteries of our solar system. A new study has proposed the possible existence of a distant world, nicknamed Planet X2 (PX2), which could help explain the unusual movements and orbital patterns of icy objects in the outer reaches of the Solar System.The research, led by University of Southern Queensland Adjunct Associate Professor Patryk Sofia Lykawka, suggests that the hypothetical planet could have a mass around 1.5 to 2 times that of Earth. Although it has not yet been directly observed, computer simulations indicate that its gravitational influence could account for several puzzling features of distant objects beyond Neptune.Long-standing search for undiscovered planetPublished in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the study offers a fresh perspective on the long-standing search for an undiscovered planet in the outer Solar System.According to the researchers, Planet X2 could follow a highly elliptical orbit hundreds of times farther from the Sun than Earth. Its estimated orbital semi-major axis could range between 350 and 500 astronomical units (AU), where one astronomical unit represents the average distance between Earth and the Sun.Even at its closest point to the Sun, PX2 would remain at least 200 AU away, placing it far beyond the orbit of Neptune.The proposed world is different from the widely discussed Planet Nine hypothesis, which suggests that a much more massive planet could be responsible for the unusual orbital behaviour of certain objects in the outer Solar System.Beyond Neptune lies a vast region known as the trans-Neptunian region, which contains numerous icy bodies. Many of these objects are part of the Kuiper Belt, a region that broadly extends between 38 and 50 AU from the Sun. University of Southern Queensland (UniSQ) Adjunct Associate Professor Patryk Sofia Lykawka – who is based at Kindai University in Japan – led the research into the possible world, which he and his team nicknamed ‘Planet X2’ (PX2).Proposed planet would have about 1.5 to 2 times Earth’s massThe proposed planet would have about 1.5 to 2 times Earth’s mass and orbit hundreds of times farther from the Sun than our own planet.While PX2 remains hypothetical, the research offers a new way to investigate the Solar System’s distant outskirts – and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s ongoing survey of the sky could help astronomers to test the theory.“Imagine discovering, after decades of mapping our Solar System, that another planet has been hiding from us all this time,” Associate Professor Lykawka said.“If this planet exists, it could change how we understand the history of our Solar System and how its most distant objects came to follow such unusual orbits.”However, astronomers have also discovered distant objects travelling along unusually elongated and highly inclined orbits that are difficult to explain solely through the gravitational influence of the known planets.One particularly intriguing example is Sedna, a distant icy object whose extremely elongated orbit takes it far beyond the planetary region.Scientists believe that the gravitational pull of an undiscovered planet could be influencing the movements of these objects, potentially explaining why some follow such unusual orbital paths.To investigate the possibility, the research team conducted computer simulations covering approximately 4.5 billion years of Solar System evolution.The simulations examined how a distant planet with different masses and orbital characteristics might influence the movements of icy bodies in the outer Solar System.The results suggest that PX2’s gravity could separate certain objects from Neptune’s gravitational influence and push others into unexpectedly tilted or elongated orbits.The proposed model successfully reproduces several unusual orbital patterns observed among distant trans-Neptunian objects. However, researchers acknowledge that some differences remain between the simulations and actual astronomical observations.

title: China's Xiaomi SU7 Ultra hits 217 mph as Electric Supercar Brand enters UAE
content: Chinese giant Xiaomi has begun selling its electric vehicles outside China for the first time, choosing the UAE as the starting point for its international expansion. The company is entering the market through local distributor Gargash Prime Automotive, with its first customer deliveries scheduled for December 2026.The UAE launch includes three model lines: the SU7 electric sedan, the YU7 SUV and the Skynomad extended-range electric SUV. Gargash Prime Automotive is offering 13 variants, with the move marking an important step in Xiaomi’s ambition to become an international automotive brand. Xiaomi’s CEO Lei Jun previously confirmed that the company plans to enter Western car markets in 2027, with Europe among its intended destinations. The UAE is a notable first market, particularly for the SU7 Ultra, a high-performance electric sedan with a three-motor powertrain producing a combined 1,548 horsepower.SU7 Ultra delivers 1,548 hp and a 217-mph top speedThe SU7 Ultra is the performance flagship of Xiaomi’s electric vehicle lineup. Its three high-torque electric motors deliver a combined 1,548 hp, allowing the sedan to accelerate from zero to 62 mph in less than two seconds. Xiaomi’s flagship model has a claimed top speed of 217 mph.Beyond straight-line acceleration, the SU7 Ultra features hardware intended for track driving. Its equipment includes carbon-ceramic brakes, a composite aerodynamic package and a large rear wing designed to generate additional downforce at speed, Electrek reported.The chassis has also been tuned for high-performance driving, with development work targeting the Nürburgring Nordschleife in Germany, one of the industry’s most demanding testing circuits.The car’s aerodynamic package has attracted attention, although some elements have also generated controversy among owners.The SU7 Ultra’s performance positioning nevertheless gives Xiaomi a high-profile model for entering markets where premium sports cars and high-performance vehicles have an established customer base. Furthermore, the SU7 Ultra will compete in a segment where buyers have access to established luxury and performance brands, while offering electric power and supercar-level acceleration.Global expansion follows rapid growth in China’s EV marketThe initial delivery schedule covers the SU7 Standard and Ultra, YU7 Standard and Skynomad N70 Pro, with customer deliveries expected to begin in December 2026. Deliveries of the remaining variants are scheduled for February 2027.The lineup gives Xiaomi an entry into several segments, from electric sedans and performance cars to SUVs with extended-range powertrains. The company has not yet disclosed a detailed timetable for introducing its vehicles in other Gulf markets, including Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. The UAE launch also provides Xiaomi with an opportunity to test its international distribution strategy through an established local automotive partner before expanding into additional markets. Xiaomi’s international ambitions come after a rapid expansion of its automotive business in China, where the company has moved beyond its traditional consumer electronics and smartphone operations. The planned 2027 expansion into Western markets will be a more demanding test, with Xiaomi needing to establish sales and service networks, meet local regulatory requirements and compete with automakers that have decades of experience in international markets.

title: Crack reopening inside one of Earth's oldest continents
content: In April 2017, a magnitude 6.5 earthquake struck eastern Botswana, shaking a part of Africa that geologists thought was among the least likely places to experience such activity. The earthquake occurred deep inside the Kalahari Craton, an ancient block of continental crust containing rocks up to 3.7 billion years old, similar to other ancient geological formations that preserve clues to Earth’s earliest history. Now, a new study suggests that the craton is being pulled apart along a geological fracture that first opened roughly 180 million years ago. The old rift went dormant, but the forces stretching eastern Africa appear to be reactivating it, raising questions about how continents break apart and whether even their oldest foundations are as stable as scientists once believed.A failed rift gets a second chanceContinental rifts form when tectonic forces pull a landmass in opposite directions, stretching and thinning its crust. If the process continues, the continent can eventually split, allowing an ocean to develop between the separating landmasses. However, these fractures usually develop in younger, weaker geological regions rather than ancient cratons, whose thick, cold and rigid interiors resist deformation. Researchers have also investigated how deep forces within Earth influence continental rifting.The new research work challenges this expectation. Published in Tectonics, the study identifies an active rift extending into the Kalahari Craton, at the southern end of the East African Rift System.“The earthquake happened in the middle of the craton, a region where no one expected to have an active fault slipping, let alone an active plate boundary developing,” Folarin Kolawole, one of the study authors and a geologist at Columbia University, said.Earlier investigations of the 2017 earthquake had already suggested that the East African Rift System extended nearly 320 kilometers (200 miles) beyond its previously recognized southern limit in northern Botswana’s Okavango Rift Zone. The new study investigates how this extension is developing and whether the structures responsible for it existed long before the recent earthquakes.Reading the rocksRift zones in East Africa. Source: Kgosidintsi et al.The researchers concentrated on the Khurutshe Fault, which produces an approximately 80-kilometer-long (50-mile) scarp across Botswana’s otherwise relatively flat landscape. The ground on one side of this geological step rises as much as 120 meters (400 feet) above the other. Similar ancient faults can remain hidden beneath landscapes, making geological mapping important for identifying their activity.To investigate what was happening underground, the team dug trenches across the fault and examined excavations made for a government water pipeline. They also used electrical resistivity tomography, a technique that sends electrical currents through the ground and measures how different underground materials resist them. The researchers combined these images with records from 20 groundwater boreholes.The imaging revealed three main geological layers. The uppermost, approximately 10 meters thick, consists of relatively young Holocene Kalahari sediments. Beneath it lies an approximately 80-meter-thick, highly discontinuous Jurassic unit containing basalts and siliciclastic rocks. The deepest layer is the much older Precambrian basement.Both the young sediments and Jurassic rocks thicken toward the fault, suggesting that the ground on one side had dropped and created space for sediment to accumulate. The trenches provided further clues: researchers found hard Jurassic sandstone containing networks of white calcite veins deposited by hot fluids moving through cracks. Polished and scratched rock surfaces also recorded earlier movement along the fault.Together, the evidence points to an initial phase of rifting during the Jurassic Period, around 180 million years ago, when parts of the continent were being stretched. Faulting began before Jurassic volcanic activity reached the area, suggesting that rising magma did not initiate the original fracture. The rift subsequently became inactive before the East African Rift System began pulling on the region again.The fault has also displaced younger Kalahari sands deposited mostly within the last 2.6 million years, indicating that movement has resumed in relatively recent geological history. Exactly when the reactivation began remains unknown.“We believe Khurutshe is one of the failed Mesozoic rifts within the craton and is reactivating,” Boniface Kgosidintsi, first author of the study and a researcher at Botswana International University of Science and Technology, said..The cracks beneath ancient rockThe discovery also offers clues about why the rift developed where it did. Instead of creating an entirely new fracture, the stretching appears to have exploited an ancient geological seam where the oldest pieces of the Kalahari Craton joined billions of years ago. “While cratons are regarded as strong old continental blocks, they do have inherent zones of weakness that can localize a new plate boundary,” Kolawole said. He adds that reactivating these structures repeatedly may be necessary before a continent can finally break apart. “Maybe you need to reactivate the rift multiple times. You need to try multiple times before it actually succeeds.”Could Africa’s plates split further?The findings could also change how scientists understand the tectonic arrangement of southern Africa. Some researchers have proposed that the region forms a relatively stable microplate called the San Plate. However, the newly identified active rift suggests this supposedly coherent block may already be separating into two smaller pieces, which the researchers call the North San Plate and South San Plate.“We cannot assume that the plate is coherent,” Kolawole said.That does not mean a new ocean is about to appear. GPS measurements indicate that southern Africa’s rifts are spreading much more slowly than more developed sections of the East African Rift System in Malawi, Kenya and Ethiopia. Some rifts never progress beyond their initial stages and eventually become inactive again. The East African Rift’s ongoing tectonic activity offers another example of the forces gradually pulling the continent apart.Any potential breakup would take millions of years, if it happens at all. Scientists still need to establish how the reactivated fault is evolving, how much further the rift may extend and whether the slowly developing fracture can eventually become a fully developed plate boundary. Nevertheless, studying this early stage could help scientists understand where future plate boundaries develop and how continents eventually divide. As Kolawole puts it, “These systems are like cracks breaking through continents, and they will determine the location and the axis of a future ocean,” he said.The study is published in the journal Tectonics.

title: US Navy plan drops DDG(X), adds 15 new 35,000-ton nuclear battleships

政策分类依据: 美国海军2027财年造舰计划提出以15艘新型核动力战列舰替代DDG(X)的量化建设目标与采购时间表，属中长期规划目标
content: A proposed overhaul of the US Navy’s future surface fleet would likely replace the planned DDG(X) destroyer program with 15 Trump-class nuclear-powered guided-missile battleships, each displacing about 35,000 tons, according to a Congressional Budget Office (CBO) latest review of the Navy’s fiscal year 2027 shipbuilding plan.Instead of procuring the next-generation DDG(X), the November 19 proposal envisions a force built around much larger capital ships equipped with hypersonic missiles, directed-energy weapons, and nuclear propulsion. According to the CBO, the Navy would procure the lead battleship in fiscal year 2028 before acquiring another ship every other year through 2056.The report estimates that the lead vessel alone would cost about $23.4 billion, while the remaining 14 ships would average roughly $18 billion each. This brings the total cost of building 15 of these Trump-class warships to an estimated $275 billion. This excludes research and development spending.Designed as capital shipThe proposed battleships, designated BBGN, would be among the largest surface combatants the US Navy has built since the Iowa class. Each vessel could reportedly displace 35,000 tons and combine a large missile battery with nuclear endurance intended for long-term operations across the Indo-Pacific.According to the proposal reviewed by the CBO, each ship would carry 128 Mk 41 Vertical Launch System cells alongside 12 Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic missiles housed in four large launch tubes. Future upgrades could also include high-energy laser weapons, an electromagnetic railgun, and a larger version of the AN/SPY-6 radar, although the CBO noted that some of those technologies may not be mature when construction begins.The Navy’s concept would also shift away from the DDG(X), originally conceived as the service’s next-generation large surface combatant, toward fewer but significantly larger and more heavily armed vessels.Battleship supersedes DDG(X)Instead of procuring DDG(X) destroyers, the alternative fleet architecture would expand the planned Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer fleet from 23 ships in the 2025 shipbuilding plan to 57, while also adding 15 nuclear-powered battleships, according to the latest analysis of the Navy’s Fiscal Year 2027 Shipbuilding Plan.The proposal is one of several force structure options assessed in the Navy’s long-term shipbuilding plan rather than an approved acquisition program.According to the CBO, the Navy’s overall 30-year shipbuilding plan would grow the battle force fleet from 286 ships today to 398 ships by 2056 through the acquisition of 371 battle force and logistics vessels.Industrial challenges remainAlthough the US Navy proposed the plan in August this year, CBO cautioned that building the battleships would bring significant industrial challenges. Newport News Shipbuilding is currently the only US shipyard capable of building nuclear-powered surface combatants, although other yards could fabricate modules before final assembly.The report also noted that concentrating large numbers of missiles aboard a relatively small fleet of capital ships could run counter to the Navy’s wider effort to distribute combat power across more surface combatants and unmanned platforms. Another shortcoming highlighted by the congressional report is the maturity of emerging technologies such as railguns and high-energy lasers that are planned to be integrated into these battleships.If pursued, the proposal would represent the Navy’s most ambitious return to heavily armed capital ships in decades, likely to replace the DDG(X) concept with a new class of nuclear-powered battleships designed for long-range operations and high-volume missile warfare.

title: Alcohol shortened survival on immunotherapy from 86 days to 58 days in mice
content: Alcohol may seriously reduce the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy, according to new research. A study published in Science Signaling found that moderate-to-heavy alcohol consumption reduced the effectiveness of cancer drugs by approximately 50 percent in mice with lung and bladder cancer.These drugs are “immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs),” so they help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. Turns out, alcohol might dull more than just our senses. Regular drinking was associated with reduced survival benefits among lung cancer patients receiving immunotherapy.“The findings together suggest that regular alcohol use can impair the efficacy of ICI against cancer,” the researchers wrote.Alcohol and cancer treatmentImmune checkpoint inhibitors help the immune system attack cancer by blocking proteins that restrict immune cell activity.One treatment, anti-PD1 immunotherapy, targets a protein called programmed cell death protein 1. These treatments have improved outcomes for patients with advanced cancers, but fewer than 30 percent achieve a durable response across most tumor types, according to the study.“By defining how modifiable risk factors affect ICI response, recommendations can be established to improve the likelihood of durable response to ICI,” the researchers wrote.To investigate these effects, researchers gave mice moderate or heavy amounts of ethanol for five weeks before introducing lung or bladder cancer cells. Then, researchers gave the mice immunotherapy while monitoring tumor growth, survival, and recurrence.In mice with lung cancer, immunotherapy extended median survival from approximately 30 to 86 days without alcohol exposure. With alcohol exposure, median survival was 58 days. In the mice with bladder cancer, immunotherapy increased survival from 22.2 percent to 88.9 percent, but alcohol reduced survival to below 30 percent.“In both models, ethanol did not affect survival in the absence of ICI, indicating a disruption of antitumor immunity,” the researchers wrote.Humans showed similar patternsThe researchers then turned to medical records. They examined patients who received anti-PD1 treatment at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Cancer Hospital between 2014 and 2018.Patients were classified as occasional drinkers, consuming less than one drink weekly, or regular drinkers, averaging about eight drinks per week. Among 93 lung cancer patients, regular alcohol consumption was significantly associated with reduced survival following immunotherapy.Findings for bladder cancer were less conclusive. Researchers found no significant effect on survival after treatment began among patients with melanoma or head and neck cancer.Alcohol weakens immune systemFurther experiments revealed that alcohol reduced the number of T cells entering tumors and impaired the activity of CD8+ T cells, which help destroy cancer cells. Alcohol exposure also increased the presence of TIGIT, a protein that inhibits immune cell activity.Researchers tested whether blocking TIGIT alongside PD1 could improve treatment outcomes.In alcohol-exposed mice, combining anti-PD1 therapy with antibodies targeting TIGIT restored treatment responses to nearly those observed in mice without alcohol exposure. Complete tumor responses reached 55.5 percent in alcohol-exposed mice receiving the combination, compared with 60 percent in controls.The researchers emphasized that their human analysis was limited by small patient samples, incomplete alcohol consumption records, and insufficient tumor immune data. They called for prospective clinical studies to determine how drinking frequency and quantity affect outcomes across different cancers.But already, the findings suggest that regular alcohol consumption can interfere with cancer immunotherapy and that TIGIT could improve treatment effectiveness.

title: Review maps what perovskite solar cells need before they can power city facades at scale
content:
Review maps what perovskite solar cells need before they can power city facades at scale
A review by researchers at Tsinghua University's Shenzhen International Graduate School, Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen),
Microquanta Semiconductor
, China State Construction Engineering Corporation Science and Industry, Zhejiang Sci-Tech University, Central South University and China Construction Eighth Engineering Division assesses perovskite solar cells for building-integrated PV (BIPV). It benchmarks them against crystalline silicon and thin-film technologies at the building and city scales. The authors screened 2,431 records and based the synthesis on 127 references.
The case for perovskites is architectural. Their areal density can be as low as about 0.2 kg/m², against roughly 12-20 kg/m² for silicon modules. Their band gap is tunable, and they can be made semi-transparent and color-neutral. In dense cities, the review notes, facades outnumber roofs. It cites an estimate that facade area is about 2.5 times rooftop area across 361 Chinese cities. Perovskites also lose less efficiency to heat, with a temperature coefficient of about -0.25%/K against -0.45%/K for silicon, and they hold up better in low light. The review reports solar heat gain coefficients of 0.14-0.33 for perovskite glazing, among the lowest of the PV glazing technologies it compared.
The review also points out that material promise is not the same as deployability. Perovskite modules still lose efficiency when scaled from cells to architectural formats. The building industry expects service lives beyond 25 years with degradation below 0.5% per year, and perovskites face the most pronounced stability challenge among the technologies compared. Long-term outdoor validation under real building conditions is lacking. The authors cite a manufacturing cost of about $0.57/W on a 100 MW line in China, with projections of $0.22-0.25/W at scale.
Lead is another concern. The review says the amount in a perovskite layer is below one tenth of the lead in the solder and pastes of a silicon module, but it exists as water-soluble salts. The authors say no study has modeled the path from an encapsulation breach to runoff in a dense city.
The authors propose a dependency-sequenced roadmap. First comes closing the cell-to-module validation gap with large-area outdoor data. Then durability testing under urban conditions and perovskite-specific certification standards must advance together, since IEC 61215 has no protocols for halide migration or lead containment. Simulation tools and system integration come last. They estimate that durability and certification will take a 5- to 10-year program.
Microquanta, which contributed an author, has
completed a light-transmitting perovskite rooftop project in Shenchi County
unveiled colored perovskite-silicon tandem BIPV modules
. The review also cites its 2026 BIPV roof for the main pavilion at the Wenzhou Garden Expo Park.

title: Chelating molecule at the interface lifts perovskite cell efficiency from 23.68% to 26.56%
content:
Chelating molecule at the interface lifts perovskite cell efficiency from 23.68% to 26.56%
Researchers at Zhengzhou University and the Institute of Chemistry of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed an interface treatment for formamidinium-based perovskite solar cells that raised the champion efficiency from 23.68% to 26.56%. The treatment uses benzeneseleninic acid (PSA), a molecule that is applied to the perovskite surface after film formation.
(g) PSA binds under-coordinated Pb²⁺ to form a Pb–O–Se chelate complex. (h) Spin-coating and annealing leave PSA molecules anchored at the perovskite surface, with outward-facing phenyl groups blocking oxygen and water. Image credit: Zhang et al., Materials Futures (2026)
Interfacial instability is a key obstacle to deploying perovskite cells. It often comes from metastable residual PbI₂, which is common after two-step deposition, and from under-coordinated Pb²⁺ ions that act as deep defects. According to the team, PSA addresses both. Its seleninic acid group loses a proton and binds to lead through two oxygen atoms, forming Pb-O-Se chelate structures. This passivates the defects and chemically converts the excess PbI₂. The molecules also assemble with their phenyl groups pointing outward, forming a hydrophobic barrier against moisture and oxygen. Hydrogen bonding with the formamidinium cations helps stabilize the halide framework and suppress ion migration.
The treated films showed a larger average grain size, lower surface roughness (28.8 nm versus 44.7 nm) and a carrier lifetime that rose from about 144 ns to 330 ns. Trap density fell by about 23%. The water contact angle increased from 55.6° to 95.3°.
The team built ITO/SnO₂/FAPbI₃/spiro-OMeTAD/Au cells with a 0.04 cm² active area. The champion PSA-treated cell reached 26.56%, with open-circuit voltage up from 1.162 V to 1.195 V and fill factor up from 78.72% to 84.58%. The hysteresis factor dropped from 2.5% to 0.8%.
Stability was tested without encapsulation. After 2,000 hours at 25 °C and 60% relative humidity, the PSA-treated cells kept 87.8% of their initial efficiency. Control cells fell to 47.1% within 1,000 hours. After 1,600 hours at 65 °C in a nitrogen atmosphere, treated cells kept 82.6%, against 50.6% for the control. In dark storage at 10% humidity for 2,000 hours, they kept 91.4%, against 60.6%.
The team plans to extend the approach to benzeneseleninic acid derivatives and selenium-containing polymer ligands, apply it to buried interfaces and other perovskite compositions, and use density functional theory calculations to screen further ligands.

content:
为落实《电力重大事故隐患判定标准及治理监督管理规定》有关要求，近日，山东能源监管办在前期排查工作基础上，进一步组织开展220千伏及以上风电、光伏及电化学储能电站重大事故隐患专项排查，共涉及269座场站，着力摸清重大事故隐患底数，提升重大事故隐患排查治理的精准性和有效性。
排查过程中，山东能源监管办聚焦新老技术标准适用、部分新投运场站设备调试及涉网试验等重点问题，逐站核实场站建设投运时间、适用技术标准、涉网性能及相关试验完成情况，结合实际逐一分析研判，确保重大事故隐患判定准确、整改依据充分。经排查，
共有82座场站存在电力重大事故隐患
。针对排查发现的隐患，督促有关企业坚持“一站一策”，结合场站实际逐一明确整改措施、责任和时限，分类推进重大事故隐患治理。目前，
63座重大事故隐患场站正在推进整改
。对尚未启动整改及治理周期较长的场站，持续加强跟踪督促，推动风险防控措施落实到位，确保重大事故隐患治理有序推进。
下一步，山东能源监管办将坚持严格监管与服务指导相结合，持续跟踪重大事故隐患整改进展，协调解决治理中的实际困难，督促有关企业压实整改责任、落实风险防控措施，推动重大事故隐患治理取得实效，切实保障电网安全稳定运行。

title: First foundations for Nordseecluster B arrive at Eemshaven
content:
The first 10 foundations for the Nordseecluster
offshore wind farm have arrived in Eemshaven, the Netherlands.
Tobias Keitel, CEO of RWE Offshore Wind, said: "The arrival of the
first monopiles for the second phase marks an important milestone in the
development of Nordseecluster."
Adding: "During construction, we need large storage areas and efficient
port infrastructure, both of which are provided by the Buss Terminal in
Eemshaven."
A total of 60 monopile foundations will be handled at Buss Ports' heavy-lift
terminal in Eemshaven this year and next. Manufactured and supplied by
Dajin Heavy Industry, the foundations are 81 metres long and weigh 1,350
tonnes each.
The Nordseecluster offshore wind project is being developed in two phases.
Nordseecluster
a capacity of 660 MW, is scheduled to become operational in early 2027.
Nordseecluster B will add a further 900 MW when it begins operations in
RWE has already secured a power purchase agreement with Amazon for 110
MW of electricity from Nordseecluster B.
