title: Cable landing works begin in Germany for NeuConnect interconnector
content:
Cable landing works begin in Germany for NeuConnect interconnector TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Cable landing works begin in Germany for NeuConnect interconnector
Cable landing works are officially underway for NeuConnect, the first direct
energy link between the UK and Germany, with work now beginning in Wilhelmshaven,
Germany.
According to the project, the milestone follows continued progress on its
700 kilometre subsea cable installation programme, which reached the halfway
point earlier this year. All subsea cabling in UK waters has now been completed.
The cables are being installed by Prysmian's Ulisse cable-laying vessel,
which was designed for shallow-water operations. The company said the cable
landing works have been carefully planned to minimise impacts on the environmentally
sensitive area.
Once completed, the offshore cable will extend to Hooksiel, where onshore
cabling has already been installed to connect to a new converter station
that is currently under construction.
NeuConnect CEO Arnaud Grévoz said: "With our subsea cabling programme
well over the halfway point, the start of cable landing works in Germany
marks another important milestone. At both ends of the project, we can
see this vital new UK German energy link continue to take shape, and we
remain firmly on track."
Once complete, NeuConnect will be one of the world's largest energy interconnectors,
spanning approximately 725 kilometres across land and sea. The link will
enable the transfer of up to 1.4 GW of electricity between two of Europe's
largest energy markets, enough to power around 1.5 million homes.

title: B.Grimm Power advances South Korean offshore wind projects
content:
The 364.8 MW Yeonggwang
Nakwol Offshore Wind Power Project
(Nakwol Project) has officially entered full commercial operation in South
Korea after completing final pre-operation inspections.
According to the announcement the project began exporting electricity to
the grid at its full capacity on 18 November and is now one of the country's
largest operating offshore wind farms.
B.Grimm Power, through its subsidiary B.Grimm Power Korea, holds a 49%
stake in the offshore project. Located off Yeonggwang County in South Jeolla
Province, Nakwol is comprised of 64 turbines with 5.7 MW of individual
capacity.
The company also announced that the neighbouring 340 MW Hanbit
offshore wind project
has signed renewable energy certificate (REC) sale and purchase agreements
covering its full output. The 20 year agreements were signed with Korea
Western Power, Korea South-East Power and Korea District Heating Corporation.
Hanbit, in which B.Grimm Power Korea also holds a 49% interest, is currently
in the early stages of construction and is targeting commercial operation
in December 2029.
The project is located adjacent to Nakwol and was selected in South Korea's
first-half 2026 fixed-price REC auction.

title: DNV awards Design Compliance Statement for 495 MW Formosa 4 wind farm
content:
The 495 MW Formosa 4 offshore wind farm has been awarded a Design Evaluation
Statement of Compliance by DNV for the project's wind turbine generator
support structures.
The certification confirms that the design meets the required standards,
allowing the project to advance to the next stage of development.
DNV issued the statement following an independent assessment of the support
structure design against international standards and project-specific requirements.
The evaluation was conducted to identify potential risks and verify compliance
with the project's technical and safety criteria.
"We value DNV's technical expertise and collaborative approach as
we work to deliver reliable renewable energy for Taiwan," said Robert
Anderson, project director for Formosa 4 at Synera Renewable Energy.
Located off the coast of Miaoli County in western Taiwan, the Formosa 4
offshore wind farm will comprise 35 turbines, each with a capacity of 14
MW to 15 MW. Once operational, the project is expected to generate enough
renewable electricity to power approximately 500,000 households.
Mette Redanz, vice president of Renewables Certification at DNV, said the
certification demonstrates that critical infrastructure has been designed
to meet the project's specific requirements and site conditions.
"It shows that critical infrastructure has been designed for the project's
specific requirements and site conditions, enabling developers, investors
and other stakeholders to manage risk and make informed decisions,"
Redanz said.

New York awards $228 million to five maritime infrastructure projects TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
New York awards $228 million to five maritime infrastructure projects
New York has announced $228 million in funding for five maritime infrastructure
projects designed to strengthen the state's ports, shipyards and waterfront
facilities while supporting the continued growth of the offshore wind industry.
The investment, awarded through the first round of New York's Port Infrastructure
Request for Proposals programme, is expected to create more than 1,000
jobs and deliver long-term economic benefits across the state.
New York State Department of Environmental Conservation Commissioner Amanda
Lefton said: "Strategic investments to upgrade New York's waterfront
ports are critical for the continued expansion of offshore wind, helping
create local jobs and support the expansion of renewable energy."
Governor Kathy Hochul said the funding supports the state's Clean, Highly
Affordable, Reliable Grid Expansion (CHARGE) agenda, which aims to accelerate
the development of renewable energy infrastructure and strengthen New York's
clean energy supply chain.
The largest award, worth $100 million, was granted to the Port of Coeymans
to expand its heavy-lift and fabrication capabilities. A further $94.8
million will support the development of the Empire Terminal at the Port
of Albany.
Other recipients include Derecktor Shipyards, which received $16.7 million
to modernise and expand its operations, and Kalypso, which was awarded
$11.8 million to establish the East Coast's first subsea cable operations
and maintenance hub. Ionic Order secured $5 million to increase waterfront
manufacturing capacity in support of offshore wind and wider marine infrastructure
projects.
Work on the projects is expected to begin immediately, with final proposals
for the second round of funding due on 26 January 2027.

title: Why Anthropic’s Math Breakthrough Matters; Why Palo Alto Networks Bought Applied Compute
content: Silicon Valley loves a good oust-and-reinstate moment. The latest example: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The chipmaker announced Monday morning that Huang, who had resigned earlier this month after reports emerged about inappropriate relationships with a supplier and employees, would return as its president, CEO and board member. It’s not clear yet what led to his reinstatement. It seems like the U.S. government was involved or at least knew ahead of the announcement that Huang would return: President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social after the announcement that the “Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO” and that “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.” Onto today’s column… Anthropic did well last week. It went public, turning many of its employees into multimillionaires and billionaires ( whether they stick around, though, is another question ). Then on Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed to have solved the most famous open problem in math, the Riemann Hypothesis , using Claude . (On Saturday, two independent groups—the Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative —verified that Alpöge’s solution was correct.) The discovery sent other AI researchers and mathematicians into a tizzy, adding to an already disorienting year of AI invasions to their turf. Until recently, little progress had been made on the 167-year-old problem, which is a conjecture that the seemingly random appearance of prime numbers actually follows a deep, hidden pattern. Then, in August, Anthropic used an unreleased version of Claude to make progress on a related problem . In October, OpenAI said that it had solved a weaker version of the Riemann Hypothesis as part of a large batch of AI-generated mathematical proofs. Researchers I spoke with told me that while Anthropic’s latest solution for Riemann won’t have a major, real-world impact, it’s another sign of the superhuman capabilities of frontier AI models in certain fields. AI excels in math in particular for a multitude of reasons, as we previously explained —including its ability to do the heavy-duty number crunching that would take humans years to do. It’s also persistent and capable of handling lots of parameters simultaneously with relative ease, and it doesn’t fall prey to the psychological biases that afflict humans. So the latest results will be sure to give mathematicians even more anxiety about the future of their field—an anxiety that is sure to carry over to experts in other fields that AI is beginning to excel at including cybersecurity and finance. Here’s what else is going on… Behind The Palo Alto-Applied Compute Deal Last week, cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks announced its intention to acquire Applied Compute , a young startup that helps companies run and customize open-source models with their own data, for $4.5 billion in stock. (The deal was yet another win for The Information 50 , our annual list of the most promising startups below a certain valuation. Applied Compute was in last year’s edition. ) Initially, the deal felt a bit random: why would a cybersecurity company like Palo Alto Networks be interested in a model training and inference startup like Applied Compute? One reason is that Palo Alto wants to get in on the business of inference, or helping developers tweak and run open-source models, a person with knowledge of the deal told me. In the aftermath of the recent Fireworks hack , in which customer data were exposed, the cybersecurity company has realized how important the market is and believes its security focus can be a differentiator. (Ironically, Palo Alto Networks’ internal threat intelligence and security consulting division Unit 42 is working with Fireworks to investigate the hack.) As to why Applied Compute founders took the deal, that’s a lot simpler. The company has only been around for 17 months and was last valued at $3.25 billion. A $4.5 billion price tag in that short amount of time is a great outcome, especially for its young founders who I imagine will be quite well off financially after this deal. Here’s what else is going on… Overheard OpenAI ’s chief scientist called for leading AI model developers to agree on limits that they won’t cross “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieve a certain concrete milestone.” “I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it,” Jakub Pachocki said in a blog post published Sunday. Policy Watch A group of over two dozen U.S. House members are forming a bipartisan caucus on AI, to be called the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus . The group will seek to balance creating AI safeguards with U.S. innovation and leadership in the technology, POLITICO reported. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Oracle on Friday announced that it had “secured all the funding we need to fulfil our contract with OpenAI ,” implying that it had raised $20 billion of additional equity and debt the company said last month it was planning “as early as” this year. Databricks , which sells data and AI software to businesses, is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at a valuation of about $225 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported. Amazon is nearing a deal to buy Decart , an Israeli AI startup developing video models, for $7.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on Saturday. Nvidia is in advanced talks to acquire Inception , which makes a faster type of AI language model, for at least $500 million plus performance-based awards for its employees, The Information reported . Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Terra Security , which uses AI agents to test companies’ cyber defenses, in a deal worth hundreds of millions of dollars that could top $500 million, Calcalist reported. Simplexity Robotics , which makes humanoid robots, raised $100 million at a $1.6 billion valuation in a pre-series A funding round led by Ant Group. Everful , which uses AI agents to help retailers source from factories, raised $48.5 million in a series A funding round led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital. Yuanshi Technology (MetaIntelli Tech), which builds AI models of cells for drug research, raised nearly 300 million yuan (about $42 million) in a pre-series A funding round led by Legend Capital . Promise Robotics , a Toronto-based company that uses AI and robotics to manufacture components for homebuilders, raised $27.9 million in Series B funding led by White Star Capital . Pragmatik Labs , an AI startup founded by Alibaba's former AI chief Lin Junyang , raised tens of millions of dollars at a $5 billion valuation, Bloomberg reported. Nodal Networks , which uses AI to plan work at shipping ports, raised $11.3 million in a seed funding round led by Eniac Ventures. Archer , formerly hackajob, which makes an AI recruiting agent, raised $10 million in a funding round led by Volition Capital. Anthropic shares fell 10% Friday, paring some of their first day of gains as a public company. After closing at a stock price of $97.17 Thursday, which was 17% above its IPO price, Anthropic shares dropped to $87 by late in the regular session Friday. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge also claimed to have solved the most famous open problem in math with help from Anthropic’s AI models. OpenAI shared new metrics on how well its models predict data, called perplexity. The company urged for the measure to be used as part of the basis for pacing the speed of AI progress and inform shared safety standards between AI developers. AI nonprofit METR said Friday it found that recent AI models, including OpenAI ’s GPT-6 Astra , are able to complete tasks that would take a human around a full work week to do . AI capabilities have continued doubling every 3.6 months, METR said. Apple is developing an AI agent that can browse the web, use apps, and write code, according to recent job postings. The iPhone maker is building an AI assistant that can use a computer much like a person does, the postings say. title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang
content: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday morning, after “senior levels of the United States government” assured Nvidia’s board that his reinstatement “poses no national security risk.” The move is an extraordinary reversal by the company’s board, whose chair Harvey Jones just six days ago had ruled out bringing Huang back. But it followed days of pressure from President Donald Trump, employees and some investors, as well as other observers such as Elon Musk. Nvidia’s stock had fallen 48% from a high in early October to as low as $125 on Friday, wiping $2.4 trillion off its market value. The stock jumped 32% in early market trading on Monday. Huang’s reinstatement looks likely to stabilize the mood on Wall Street about the durability of the AI boom. Nvidia had pumped tens of billions into a wide array of neoclouds and AI companies, helping drive demand for its chips and fuel expansion of data centers to serve AI. Rising interest rates in recent weeks had sparked questions about the durability of the boom and those questions intensified after Huang departed Nvidia. On Friday, AI-related stocks fell sharply. Stocks reversed course on Monday: neoclouds such as Coreweave and Nebius jumped more than 20%. Minutes after Nvidia’s announcement went out, President Trump endorsed it, posting on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision” in reinstating Huang. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Trump wrote. He added that the U.S. government has “no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security,” and that the U.S. Attorney General has confirmed that the government doesn’t have evidence that Huang “has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” The White House later issued a statement saying “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the Nvidia board. We have to protect our geniuses.” Huang’s reinstatement raises questions about the future of Nvidia’s China business, as reports had suggested that he had facilitated smuggling of chips into China. Within Trump’s administration and the U.S. Congress, a growing chorus of China hawks had expressed concern about Huang’s conduct following his ouster. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday had said that the government “needs answers” from Nvidia about how it managed U.S export controls around chips. Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement that “a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang” had convinced the board “with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.” Jones added that the “board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.” The board has not completed its investigation of whether Huang was a target of foreign intelligence, however, and Jones said in a statement that the investigation, which is being conducted by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, will continue. Jones last week had said the board had accepted Huang’s resignation “after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.” Huang had admitted to having an affair, although he didn’t say with whom.  Reports have identified both Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. authorities believe was a Chinese spy and a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. Huang’s departure also came after a New York Times report that he had had a second affair with Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia vice president who had reported directly to him. Huang’s relationship with the former Megaspeed executive goes back several years. Alice Huang and her sister had built a network of companies that acquired billions of dollars in Nvidia chips. Some of those chips ended up in data centers that served major Chinese tech firms like Alibaba and Tencent. In 2022, Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, months before U.S. export controls on chips came into effect. Huang’s departure had prompted a major campaign to bring him back, including from President Trump , who said on Friday that he “would love to see” Jensen Huang return as Nvidia CEO. A petition to reinstate Huang had gathered more than 200,000 signatures as of Friday, including from Silicon Valley figures as Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, whose firm owns less than 0.01% of Nvidia shares. Baker also signed a separate letter with Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner urging the board not to rush to replace Huang. Other Huang supporters included Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and activist investor Bill Ackman, who has supported Huang on the social media site and criticized the board’s handling of the exit. The fallout from the Huang drama will take months to become clear. Nvidia’s board is conducting an investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, while the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating Nvidia’s accounting of its sales to China. Nvidia is also facing a U.S. Department of Justice criminal probe that focuses on chip customers that illicitly diverted chip shipments to China. Congress is also investigating: Huang is due give closed-door testimony on Dec. 1.

title: AMD’s Valuation is Getting Ahead of Its Fundamentals
content: AMD has been the darling of large-cap semiconductor investors this year, with its stock up 98% so far even after Friday’s big selloff. While some on Wall Street think the recent turmoil at Nvidia could be an opportunity for AMD to sell more of its AI chips to customers and steal market share, its valuation is already predicated on sky-high growth expectations and doesn’t reflect the geopolitical, financing and execution risks the company faces. AMD, whose chips many customers regard as cheaper, second-rate alternatives to Nvidia’s, began trading at a valuation premium to Nvidia and rival chip designer Broadcom in the second half of last year. That’s when AMD announced that it had signed a deal to give OpenAI the right to buy a substantial chunk of its shares in exchange for purchasing 6 gigawatts worth of its AI chips. AMD signed a similar deal with Meta Platforms in February this year, which has helped boost its growth projections. Analysts expect AMD will grow revenue next year by 84%, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence, ahead of Nvidia’s 75%. But that’s not as much of an achievement as it sounds. In 2022, the year that OpenAI released ChatGPT and unleashed the AI revolution, the two chip makers had almost the same revenue—AMD reported $23.6 billion while Nvidia had $26.9 billion. Over the next three years, Nvidia’s revenue mushroomed nearly tenfold, to $215.9 billion in the year ending January 2026, and it is on track to double this year. AMD, in contrast, grew much more slowly and is on track to generate just $52 billion this year. Moreover, AMD is much less profitable because its chips don’t command nearly as high a premium as Nvidia’s; its gross profit margin has hovered in the low-to-mid 50s for the last few years while Nvidia’s has exceeded 70%. Even if AMD is able to raise its prices on the back of heightened demand in the coming years, given the long-term nature of the purchasing contracts its customers sign, it’s unlikely it can do so fast enough to be on par with Nvidia anytime soon. Moreover, while Nvidia’s business dealings in China have been heavily scrutinized in the past couple of weeks—amid questions about former CEO Jensen Huang’s management—short seller Hunterbrook published a report last week noting that AMD’s  business ties to China weren’t that different. The report sent AMD shares falling 8% on Thursday, and the stock fell another 13% on Friday amid a big tech stock selloff that hit companies with AI ties the hardest. As of Friday, AMD was trading at 25 times forward earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, compared with Nvidia’s 7 times. Broadcom, which has gross margins even higher than Nvidia’s, trades at 14 times. (Nvidia stock is down 32% so far this year, while Broadcom has fallen 12%.) Even analysts who are bullish on AMD stock have expressed concern about the valuation. “We are firm believers in AMD’s revitalized product road map strategy, and product traction is compelling. However, expectations for share gains and growth are high. We’re concerned that any moderate downtick to expectations could add substantial risk to the stock based on valuation levels well above peers,” KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst John Vinh, who has an “overweight” rating on AMD, wrote in a Nov. 3 report. CPU Promise The bull case for AMD has long rested, in part, on AMD’s CPU business—the chips that help manage the operating system for servers laden with both AI and non-AI chips. As usage of agentic AI tools increases, companies need more CPUs to pair with a single AI chip to be able to perform complex tasks. That’s something both Intel—which historically dominated the market for CPUs—and AMD have called a catalyst for growth. Indeed, while AI chips such as Nvidia’s graphics processing units have been in short supply for several years, CPUs have lately also been hard to get. Moreover, AMD appears to be taking share in CPUs from Intel. Next year, Intel expects overall industry server CPU units sold to grow by more than 30%. But AMD executives said on an earnings call this month that they expect the company’s server CPU revenue to roughly double, largely as a result of selling more units, not just from increasing prices. Even better, AMD likely makes more profit on each server CPU it sells than Intel does, reckon analysts from Counterpoint Research . Picking up more CPU market share from Intel could underpin AMD’s growth next year, but the company is also relying heavily on shipments of its AI chips to fuel its growth. In the December quarter this year, the company expects sales of AI chips to surpass revenue from its server CPUs for the first time, according to its chief financial officer, Jean Hu, on the company’s November earnings call. But gangbusters growth in AMD’s AI chip business is far from guaranteed. Perhaps the biggest risk is geopolitical. Nvidia this week moved to halt sales of its H200 chips in China entirely, following reports that some of its chips ended up at firms sanctioned by the U.S. government, despite those sales being approved by the U.S. Department of Commerce. Any regulatory action to crimp U.S. firms’ chip sales to China as a result could hamper AMD’s growth there; China made up 22% of its revenue in 2025. Already, competition is steep. Broadcom, for one, is helping some of AMD’s rivals, such as Google, develop custom AI chips that are gaining traction as an alternative to Nvidia and AMD’s offerings. Nvidia’s close relationship with chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company also gives it a manufacturing capacity advantage that AMD may struggle to overcome. One company that wanted to use AMD’s AI chips ultimately decided against doing so because the wait time to procure them was significantly longer than the wait time to get Nvidia chips, The Information reported last week . “In AI training, Nvidia clearly dominates, and then AMD is trying to grow into a stronger position as a very significantly distant number two player,” said Hendi Susanto, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds who owns stock in AMD, Nvidia and Broadcom. “On AI inference, we are seeing intense competition from Nvidia, AMD and then the custom ASIC” designers, the largest of which is Broadcom. Perhaps the most notable risk to AMD’s business is similar to a risk facing Nvidia, but is more acute for AMD given its much smaller scale. AMD has entered into $28 billion worth of credit guarantees, joint leases and other support to help its customers secure data center capacity, Hunterbrook estimated in its report this week. Plus, it is on the hook for another $48.8 billion in purchase commitments to its suppliers by the end of next year, more than the $45.4 billion in revenue it generated over the last four fiscal quarters. Meanwhile, it ended the September quarter with just $6.5 billion in excess cash, after factoring in its own debt obligations. The gap between AMD’s cash reserves and cash generation, on the one hand, and its hefty obligations to customers and suppliers on the other, raise the risk for the company if AI demand cools. “There are still challenges that the AI ecosystem as a whole needs to address,” Gabelli Funds’ Susanto said. “The first one is geopolitics. The second one is AI financing, which includes vendor financing and circular financing. And then there’s the neoclouds” such as TensorWave and CoreWeave, which buy chips from AMD and Nvidia and rent them out to customers, some of which Gabelli said could fail given their “business model of needing to make significant investments before [generating] multi-year revenue streams.” While both Nvidia and AMD are exposed to these risks, AMD’s deluxe valuation, second-rate technological position and smaller cash coffers relative to its financial obligations mean it is far too soon for investors to declare it a definitive winner on the heels of its rival’s management challenges.

title: AI Bubble Deflating? Dell, Workday on Deck
content: Friday’s tech stock bloodbath prompted much gnashing of teeth over the weekend. With stocks most exposed to AI—such as Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius—falling in the 12-16% range, and Anthropic tanking on its second day of trading, it felt like the air has finally gone out of the AI bubble. Indeed, worries about AI financing are so intense that Oracle issued a statement late on Friday proclaiming that it had raised all the money it needed for its big OpenAI data center deal and any report that said otherwise was wrong—suggesting it’s a little sensitive about things. Meanwhile, The Information captured the craziness of the AI bubble with a report late Friday that SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son had explored doing a trillion dollar buyout of SK Hynix. We should emphasize ‘explored’ in past tense—SoftBank said the idea was no longer being pursued. That’s good because the idea is sheer fantasy. SoftBank’s balance sheet is already stretched, thanks to the loans it has taken out to invest in OpenAI. How would Son imagine he could raise the hundreds of billions needed to buy Hynix (leave aside the fact that the South Korean government would be unlikely to ever allow such a deal). What brand of crack is he smoking? But dealmaking in the AI world is certainly happening. The Israeli newspaper Calcalist reported late last week that Amazon was very close to finalizing a purchase of the Israeli AI firm Decart, which makes hyper-efficient-to-run video models, for $7.5 billion in cash, stock and deferred payments. Decart was an early customer of Amazon’s Trainium3 chip, we reported last December, which shows the two companies have had some business dealings. (Here’s a deep dive on Decart we published in 2024). This Week’s Earnings It takes a special devil-may-care attitude to report earnings a day or two before Thanksgiving—and perhaps not surprisingly there aren’t too many companies with that mindset. Among those in that camp is Zoom Communications, the videoconferencing firm (and Anthropic shareholder!), which reports earnings for its October quarter on Monday. Then there’s Workday, the enterprise software firm, which reports for the same period on Tuesday, along with Dell Technologies. None of these companies typically get much attention for their earnings reports, but this time may be different—and not just because there won’t be much else happening this week. Workday, Zoom and Dell each have exposure, of different kinds, to AI. Dell, for instance, is one of the major distributors of Nvidia-powered servers, which means it is part of the Nvidia gravy train of the past few years. Dell’s revenue from “AI-optimized servers” (as it calls them) jumped from $1.8 billion in fiscal 2024 to $24.7 billion in the year to January, and was up another 222% in the first half of the current fiscal year. And that’s just sales: Dell finished the July quarter with a backlog of $95 billion in AI orders, it said. And AI servers are only part of its business: the company has said its non-AI business is also doing well. Overall, Dell’s top-line growth rate has jumped from 1.1% in fiscal 2023 to 18.8% last fiscal year to 71% in the first half of this fiscal year. Analysts are projecting Dell will report 82% higher revenue for the October quarter, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. No wonder Dell’s stock is up 121% so far this year, even taking into account Friday’s big stock selloff when Dell shares fell 11%. (In this context, this Financial Times report from Sunday about the pricing policies of Dell and other server makers is worth reading). Then there’s Workday, one of those software firms vulnerable to disruption from AI alternatives (yes, the Saaspocalypse!). With that threat in mind, company co-founder Aneel Bhusri in February grabbed the CEO steering wheel of the company back from Carl Eschenbach, who had succeeded him two years before. So far, there’s little sign Bhusri has come up with a magical solution to the AI threat. Workday’s revenue growth has slowed in the first two quarters of this fiscal year, after a pickup at the end of last year. Analysts are projecting that top-line growth will slow again, to 10.6%, in the fiscal third quarter, ending Oct. 31, according to S&P data. As for Zoom, its business was barely growing even before AI became a thing—and it continues to chug along at a 4% to 5% annual rate. But Zoom has a stake in Anthropic worth close to $5 billion at Anthropic’s IPO price, which is about 20% of its market capitalization. That’s big enough that it deserves more attention from investors! In Other News • CrowdStrike is in talks to buy Zscaler, Bloomberg reported on Friday, a deal that would cost tens of billions of dollars. Zscaler has a market capitalization of $32 billion. • Marc Lore’s Wonder is trying to sell Grubhub, the Wall Street Journal reported , just weeks after Amazon replaced Grubhub with Uber Eats as Prime’s food delivery offering. • OpenAI’s chief scientist called for leading AI model developers to agree on limits that they won’t cross “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieve a certain concrete milestone.” Friday on The Information’s TITV Check out Friday's episode of TITV in which Akash and Martin analyze Anthropic’s IPO performance. title: Exclusive: Making Hay From a Scarcity in the World of Robotaxis—Places to Service Them
content: In the late 2010s, when Neha Palmer was head of energy strategy at Google, she frequently came across electric vehicle developers that aimed to manufacture and sell hundreds of thousands of cars. They envisaged their customers as fleet owners who would save tons of operating expenses if they didn’t have to buy fuel. But Palmer always had a nagging question: How would the fleet owners power these EVs? “Their answer was always, ‘Oh, we'll figure it out,’” she recalls. Today, as Tesla, Waymo and Amazon’s subsidiary Zoox are rolling out electric driverless robotaxis in multiple states, that question is even more pressing. For all three companies, the growth of their robotaxi fleets is sharply constrained by the paucity of places to charge the vehicles, not to mention clean and park them safely late at night, when most of them are idle. In 2021, Palmer left Google to take over as CEO of Terawatt Infrastructure, which earlier this month announced the construction of service depots for robotaxis and other large electric vehicle fleets in four U.S. cities—Dallas, Miami, Nashville, Tenn., and San Francisco. It’s a booming business, Palmer says—she plans to have nine such depots operating by the end of the year and be operating roughly 25 in all by the end of 2027. Among customers using the depots as of now are Waymo and Lyft, Terawatt says. In June, the startup raised $300 million in debt, bringing its total equity and debt fundraising to more than $1 billion. “Getting large amounts of power to sites is a bigger lift than I think anyone's giving credence to,” she told me. Terawatt and other nascent depot operators reflect the picks and shovels part of the physical AI boom. Just as men racing to participate in the California gold rush of the late 1840s had often overlooked the tools they would need to extract the metal, AI startups have neglected to consider some mundane requirements to make going concerns of humanoid robots, robotaxis, electric aircraft and other products. In the case of driverless robotaxis, no one can estimate the scale of the industry’s lapse in advance planning. Predictions of the number of robotaxis to be made in the future range from thousands of new vehicles per year to—if you are Elon Musk —millions. But suffice it to say that the shortage of parking space is large and growing quickly since both Tesla and Waymo intend to own and operate virtually all the cars themselves. Martin Viecha, who was Tesla’s vice president of investor relations until leaving the company two years ago, has founded a startup, Physical AI Data, that uses satellite imagery and other data to track and map AI robotaxi depots globally. (It also tracks global supply chains for components in other physical AI industries like drones and humanoid robots.) Speaking for the first time publicly about his startup, Viecha said the highest estimates of future robotaxi demand are the most realistic ones. But they are also the most worrying if you are thinking of being ready for them. In New York City, for example, he said, Tesla had managed to find spaces for only 14 supercharging dispensers. “That’s one-four over the last decade and a half. Why? Because it‘s nearly impossible to buy parking spaces at scale in New York,” he said. “And it’s not going to be too different in Chicago. It's not going to be too different in central Boston, et cetera, et cetera.” “To say that you're going to deploy a million robotaxis is like, ‘OK, do you have a million parking spots—overnight, secure parking spots? So not in a Walmart, but somewhere where vandals cannot get to them overnight?’” he said. But if it were just the practical matter of finding places to wash and charge these cars, the solution would be easy—you would just do it in the suburbs surrounding the big metropolitan areas. Unfortunately, it’s not that simple. Making money in the robotaxi business has everything to do with what proportion of a robotaxi’s total miles driven have a paying passenger inside. This means not wasting too many miles driving to a city from a distant suburb. Waymo, Viecha said, has done the best job of organizing close-in servicing spots for its cars. He said Waymo’s utilization rate in California is now near 60%, meaning that an average of 40% of the miles its cars in the state drive have no passenger. As a loose comparison, that’s superior to what’s happening in the human-driven ride-sharing world, in which Uber’s utilization rate is roughly 56%, Viecha said. “Robotaxi depots need to be close to where their customers are,” Viecha said. “If a robotaxi needs to drive 10 miles to reach its first morning customer and then again 10 miles back to the depot after dropping off the last customer, that's already 20 empty miles.” The availability of service depots and utilization rates are so central to robotaxi economics that they are predictors of the rate of robotaxi rollout for each company, Viecha said. For instance, Tesla’s greatest robotaxi growth is in Austin, Texas, and not in Dallas, San Francisco or cities in Florida, he said. “Why is all this growth coming out of Austin? The reason is that in Austin, they have a lot of parking locations because they have a whole factory there,” he said. Terawatt builds its depots from scratch, acquiring the land, striking power deals with utilities and building the charging infrastructure. It then leases the depot spaces to customers, including not only robotaxis but companies operating fleets of electric commercial trucks. In all, it takes the startup 18 to 24 months to develop a depot from start to finish, Palmer said. Terawatt maintains the chargers with the aim of keeping them working 99% of the time. Public charging infrastructure doesn’t work for these fleets because they need to be serviced, including repairs of anything that’s gone wrong with the vehicles, she said. Palmer noted that it took decades during the last century for oil companies to build out the current gasoline fueling infrastructure that everyone takes for granted. The development of robotaxi depots, she said, “is gonna be a really big industry.” ----- Noteworthy Elon Musk is doubling down on one of the biggest blunders of his tech career, which is getting out of the EV business—Tesla’s cash cow—and deciding to make only robotaxis, a business of the future whose ultimate scale is so far unproven. In an interview last week with journalist Andrew Ross Sorkin, Musk said that some time in the future, Tesla would remove the steering wheel and pedals from the Model Y and make it a large robotaxi. Musk’s headlong move into robotaxis has left the EV market almost entirely to Chinese carmakers. Michigan battery startup Our Next Energy said it will go public next year in a reverse merger with a special purpose acquisition company. The deal values ONE at $600 million, which if legitimate would reflect a 50% haircut from the $1.2 billion valuation it achieved in its 2023 Series B round. If it’s successful in raising tens of millions of dollars for ONE’s manufacturing buildout, the public listing would mark a significant turnaround for the startup and its founder, Mujeeb Ijaz. As we reported earlier this month , Ijaz, after being demoted to chief technology officer from CEO in 2023, has made a comeback by eschewing plans to make EV batteries and making them for locomotives and maritime drones. For the first time, Ford made and shipped finished lithium-iron-phosphate battery cells to the Kentucky plant where next year it will make its new midsize electric truck, the Fathom. Ford made the LFP cells at a Michigan plant that it has outfitted with manufacturing equipment licensed from Chinese behemoth Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd. It appears to be the first major production of LFP cells in the U.S. Ford appears to use Chinese chemicals, known as cathode active material, to make the cells, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence , a battery research firm. The drone battery boom triggered by the war in Ukraine is now generating intellectual property lawsuits: BEILab, a South Korean maker of lithium-metal batteries, has captured business powering multiple combat drones used in Ukraine, as we have reported . But Massachusetts battery developer SES AI, which is seeking to sell its own lithium metal batteries to drone customers, has sued BEI , claiming its batteries infringe on SES’s patents. title: How Amazon Plays the Long, Expensive Data Center Game That Neoclouds Can’t
content: INDIANA, Penn.—A visit this week to an Amazon data center project in Pennsylvania coal country gave me a glimpse of the era we all knew was coming: when tech giants lay claim to some of the hardest-to-secure AI infrastructure while smaller cloud providers, which Nvidia has propped up financially, are trying to hang on. The 4.4-gigawatt campus in Pennsylvania, once home to a 2-GW coal-fired power plant near the economically depressed borough of Homer City, could become one of the largest AI power parks in the country. Few companies can marshal the resources as readily as Amazon to transform the site from what it was—a Rust Belt relic that once employed thousands of people but released coal dust and arsenic—into an Appalachian hilltop of gas-fired electrons flowing into 36 buildings powering the AI of Anthropic or others. Here are some numbers to help put this project in perspective: 2036 . That’s the year Amazon expects to finish the 36th building. The campus is part of a $20 billion investment pledge in Pennsylvania, but Amazon will likely spend tens of billions of dollars more on this campus alone, including chips. (The power developer says 3.7 GW is set aside for data centers, but Amazon’s power use is not yet disclosed and there may be other tenants.) 32% . That’s the percentage of power the governor wants data centers to source from “dispatchable, clean firm” energy sources by 2035 to get faster permitting review, according to conditions that Gov. Josh Shapiro laid down in an August executive order. Amazon has not said whether it will comply with the governor’s standards, which would mean procuring nuclear, geothermal, hydropower or fossil with carbon capture. (Homer City is currently under construction as a 100% gas project.) 11 . That’s the minimum number of entities I counted that need to bless the projects in some way: three townships, two boroughs, one county commission, one planning commission, a state environmental gatekeeper, two regional grid authorities and a federal energy regulator. All of them will want something in return, whether taxes, funding for local facilities or infrastructure improvements, pledges from Amazon to pay for local power upgrades or compliance on protecting wetlands, animals and the air. Environmental groups have appealed the air pollution permit, which the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection granted in November 2025, and the case is pending before a review board. Nine . That’s the number of trade unions already involved in the power plant construction. Amazon has said it may not use union labor for all of the the data center construction, says Shawn Steffee, a business agent for the local boilermakers union and president of a regional building trades council. He says he told Amazon to do better. “If you’re going to invite us to Thanksgiving dinner, we all get a piece of turkey, or none of us are staying for dinner,” he said. Amazon will be inviting conflict if union labor that’s already at the site is displaced by out-of-state, non-union labor. (An Amazon rep told me the company values “the important contributions of skilled trades” and prioritizes local hiring.) Amazon’s power partner will need to work closely with authorities in the Mid-Atlantic grid operator, PJM Interconnection, which serves 13 states and has jurisdiction over some of the transmission lines Amazon will use to connect to the grid in a region with rising power bills and lengthy regulatory queues. Amazon has spent 29 years entering communities across the country to build fulfillment centers and cementing relationships with local economic development authorities. That has given it a huge head start opening doors, economic development officials in other states have told me. The younger cloud providers, also known as neoclouds, lack this kind of experience. Amazon is also a trusted counterparty to utilities and has the financial heft to strike novel deals, such as a recent arrangement in which Indiana state utility NIPSCO agreed to connect Amazon’s data center sites to power sooner while delivering bill credits to local ratepayers as Amazon’s usage ramps up. Josh Weissman, a vice president at Amazon Web Services, said in a statement that the company “takes a long-term approach” in building data centers. “We’re committed to engaging communities early, listening to local concerns, and investing in infrastructure and programs that deliver lasting benefits.” In addition to having some of the largest AI data centers already operating, Amazon and Google are at the top of rankings of AI data center construction starts in the past 12 months, according to new data from analytics firm Cleanview. We’d bet that some of those facilities will hold Amazon Trainium chips and Google tensor processing units rather than Nvidia GPUs. (Cleanview defines construction starts as steel, walls or columns actually going up.) Amazon in the past year started projects that could grow to 4.6 GW, and that excludes the Homer City site, which hasn’t gotten that far. Google was second in that ranking, with 4.1 GW of sites getting underway. To be sure, Nvidia and its data center and cloud partners are also moving quickly. Tech firms and developers that use its chips have started over 10 gigawatts of construction in the last 12 months, including Meta as well as developers working for Oracle, such as Vantage and Stack. Stealth Moves Amazon has been quiet about its data center work, and I don’t mean that in a good way. I attended a planning commission public hearing Wednesday night about Amazon’s land use in Indiana County, where Homer City is located, and Amazon was conspicuously absent. Ten opponents had signed up in advance to speak there, a comedown from the dozens that spoke at a past hearing. I soon understood why: the planning commission officials said they had been meeting weekly in their office with Amazon to hash out questions. That’s allowed, but it wasn’t exactly putting on the charm offensive and directly sharing its actions with community members. (The Amazon rep said its leaders “recognize that engaging directly with communities is an important part of responsible, long-term development.”) This is a tactical ground game that requires a deep well of resources. Ultimately, Amazon will almost surely dig into its deep pockets and offer ways to help the community. But it knows it will never appease national environmental groups that oppose replacing coal with another huge new source of emissions. Amazon identified itself as the patron of the Homer City campus only after a TribLive reporter forced its hand a few months ago by disclosing a 2025 exchange about the project between an Amazon executive and a state business development agency. Until then, the only entity known to be behind it was Homer City Redevelopment (HCR), a privately financed power developer whose backers include New York distressed bond investors who took ownership of the ailing coal plant in 2017. Ground Game Money has been pouring into the project all year, with the expectation of a large customer like Amazon showing up. When I visited in February, HCR was negotiating to buy farms from homeowners, an RV camp for project workers was under construction, and trucks were streaming in and out of the site, hauling away debris from the coal plant that was demolished and starting the new power plant and data center campuses. This full ground game—which is what it takes to make a project happen—isn’t apparent in the satellite images that many research firms use to update investors. The prevailing assumption about the Homer City project was that it would make its own power outside of the grid, when in fact the power developers are planning to put 100% of the power on the grid and then deliver some of it to Amazon, which is right next door. Doing so allows the developer to ease a regional power shortage that is of great concern to public officials. It’s unclear whether drawing power from the grid could allow the company to say it is complying with the 32% clean-energy requirement; roughly a third of the grid’s electrons come from nuclear. (For carbon-counting purposes, tech firms often reflect gridwide figures; Amazon is also contracting to upgrade nuclear plants in the area and stressed that it has been “the largest corporate purchaser of carbon-free energy since 2019.”) Amazon is also bankrolling bespoke gas power for a data center project in the Permian Basin in Texas; it has a 7.65 GW air pollution permit but development plans so far suggest Amazon would build closer to 5 GW or less. Just like Homer City, the Texas site sits on top of one of the most prolific gas fields in the country. But Amazon has clarified that it sees its Texas power plants there potentially becoming part of the grid in the future, saying they would add power supply to benefit other customers. These two projects are exceedingly capital intensive and could stretch for a decade. Yes, newer entrants in the data center field are getting a lot done in a relatively short time frame in places like Texas. But I have a hard time imagining them navigating a Northeastern state like Pennsylvania as easily. (Plus, financing for new projects is harder than ever for newer entrants to access at reasonable rates.) In every new data center ribbon-cutting following the Blue Tsunami election—which sent more data center skeptics into office—achieving excellent economics at scale looks like a big-company game, and it will only get more so. title: How Apple Got Caught Up in Google Search Ads Slowdown
content: Google’s shares have fallen 18% since the company reported a sharp slowdown in search advertising revenue growth stemming in part from the increased popularity of its AI features. Google isn’t the only tech company feeling the pain from that shift. Growth in Apple’s services revenue, which includes a cut of ad revenue Google makes when people search on Apple’s Safari web browser, slowed to 10% in the latest quarter from 12% in the prior quarter, and will cool further in the current quarter, executives said on Apple’s earnings call earlier this month. Reddit also warned in its latest quarterly report that Google wasn’t sending as much search referral traffic to its online forums because of AI-driven changes to search features. The reports illustrate how even small changes to Google’s search juggernaut can set off monumental ripples across a variety of companies. Google generated $187 billion in search advertising for the first nine months of this year and is the biggest seller of digital ads globally. “[Google] is not monetizing the AI Overviews as well as they did the search surface and that’s showing up to a degree in Apple’s deceleration in services,” Barton Crockett, senior research analyst at Rosenblatt Securities, said on The Information’s TITV. Although Google’s year-over-year growth in queries hit its fastest pace in five years, ad monetization was lower for searches that were in AI mode—the ChatGPT-like chatbot in its search service—than traditional search, Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said on Google’s third-quarter earnings call late last month. Search ad revenue growth slowed to 12% compared to 17% the prior quarter and 19% before that. Apple’s iPhones and other devices have long been one of the main ways users access Google search. A court witness representing Google in its antitrust trial disclosed in 2023 that Google was paying Apple 36% of the revenue it generates from such ads when people see them on Safari. Separate court filings say Google paid Apple $20 billion in 2022. It’s not clear how much Google pays Apple currently. Reddit’s Fallout Reddit generates ad revenue from internet traffic that Google directs its way. It also earns licensing fees from Google for enhanced access to Reddit content, including in its use for training Google’s AI. Reddit has been seeing less traffic from Google as AI Overviews, Google’s AI-generated summaries of search results, answers more queries directly, Reddit executives said on an earnings call Oct. 29. Reddit’s daily unique users in the U.S. dropped from 53.2 million in the second quarter of 2026 to 50.7 million in the third quarter. “This doesn’t say anything about the internet consumer’s demand for Reddit. People still want Reddit,” CEO Steve Huffman said during the earnings call. “It says Google is not sending them to Reddit the way they used to.” Reddit’s shares have fallen 34% since their Oct. 29 close, compared to 13.6% for the Nasdaq Composite index. To reduce Reddit’s reliance on Google, Huffman has said the company plans to place a larger emphasis on its app and to encourage users to access Reddit directly. Changes Ahead Google is still experimenting with ads in its AI features and has been cautious about placing too many ads or using formats that turn off users. People are also using AI search differently than regular search with broader, longer queries that don’t lead as readily to purchases. But advertisers expect that it will gradually figure out how to show ads that match queries better and will increase ads shown, which could cause growth to rebound. “We’re intentionally designing AI Search to highlight the web, providing opportunities for people to click out and helping websites build their audiences,” a Google spokesperson said in a statement. “We’re now sending billions of clicks to websites every week through our Search AI features.” That strength could benefit Apple as well—especially if even more users flock to AI Mode than have been using regular search. Morningstar senior equity analyst Ahmed Khan predicts Google will scale AI Mode first to capture more users, and then slowly introduce more ads. He expects AI Mode to reach the same level of monetization as traditional search in late 2027 or early 2028. In the longer term, Andrew Boone, an equity research analyst at investment bank Citizens, sees Google search evolving into an agentic interface integrating Google’s Gemini AI models. Google introduced Gemini-supported task automation within some Android phones in March and released its Gemini Spark AI agent in May. It released further updates , called Tasks, last week.

title: The Download: AI’s judgment problem and carbon removal’s crop threat
content:
The Download: AI’s judgment problem and carbon removal’s crop threat
Plus: AI may have cracked math's greatest unsolved problem.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some capabilities are improving exponentially—but models aren’t as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
The report updates METR’s widely shared time horizon plot, which tested models on a large suite of tasks. The new version adds more open-ended tasks, such as designing AI evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments.
Models struggled with these tasks, which could prove crucial to automating research and development.
Find out where AI progress is running into tougher challenges.
—Grace Huckins
Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
Google, Microsoft, and others are investing hundreds of millions of dollars in startups spreading crushed rock across farms to capture carbon from the air.
The approach, known as enhanced rock weathering, could also improve soil quality and boost crop yields.
But new research raises serious questions about how much material can be added to farmland before it starts reducing yields, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. The findings suggest the carbon removal potential could be far smaller than previously estimated.
Here’s why major concerns are emerging about enhanced rock weathering.
—James Temple
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

—John Kennedy, US senator from Louisiana, tells NBC’s Meet the Press that Jensen Huang’s alleged affair could prove costly for efforts to prevent China from obtaining AI chips.

He gave MIT Technology Review exclusive access to his unofficial Starlink repair workshop in the city of Lviv. Here’s what we learned.

title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
content:
Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
Spreading alkaline rock on fields to lock away carbon helps farmers at first, but new research shows that those benefits could be strictly limited.
Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.
Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.
But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.
Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.
These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.
“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”
How it works
There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.
The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.
If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.
“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.
ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.
But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.
So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).
“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”
“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”
Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.
“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.
Agricultural limits
But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.
A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.
Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.
The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.
“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”
The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.
Rising popularity
Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.
Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.
Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.
He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and academic groups.
All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.
Tempered expectations
The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.
In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.
CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.
Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.
“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”
Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post. She also criticized the nonprofit for not contacting the company before posting its results and for publishing them on a blog instead of in peer-reviewed literature.
Kukla says CarbonPlan did account for higher applications of crushed rock in its analysis.
A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.
Healthy debate
But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?
Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the company accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.
“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”
Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.
Yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the new findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.
Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.
But it’s important to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.
“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.

title: China's landmark lead-carbon storage project faces CNY 103 million battery lawsuit - Energy Storage
content: A subsidiary of China’s State Power Investment Corporation (SPIC) has filed a CNY 103.08 million ($14.4 million) lawsuit against three engineering contractors over alleged battery quality and performance problems at the Heping Gongchu (Peaceful Co-Storage) energy storage project in Zhejiang province. The lawsuit was disclosed on November 14 by Shenzhen-listed Hangzhou Gisway Information Technology Co., Ltd. (301390.SZ), whose wholly owned subsidiary is among the defendants. The plaintiff, Diantou Zhechu (Changxing) Smart Energy Co., Ltd., has sued Zhejiang Taihu Energy Valley Technology Co., Ltd., Hangzhou Hongsheng Power Design Consulting Co., Ltd., and Zhejiang Changxing Electrical Engineering Co., Ltd. The three companies formed the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) consortium that signed the contract for the project’s first phase in December 2022. According to the filing, the project owner alleges that battery equipment failed to meet contractual quality and performance requirements, resulting in insufficient electricity discharge and associated revenue losses. The plaintiff is seeking compensation for lost discharge output and related interest, battery replacement costs, legal expenses and other litigation-related charges. It argues that the three consortium members should bear joint and several liability under the EPC contract. The case has been accepted by the Changxing County People’s Court in Huzhou, but hearings have not yet begun. The dispute involves one of China’s most prominent lead-carbon battery storage demonstrations. Located in Changxing County, Huzhou, the Heping Gongchu project was planned with a total capacity of 100.8 MW/1,061.68 MWh and investment of approximately CNY 1.6 billion. Its first phase, rated at 45.36 MW/477.757 MWh, was connected to the grid in March 2023. The project’s second phase was designed for a further 583.93 MWh, although its current completion status has not been confirmed. At its launch, the development was promoted as the world’s largest single-site smart energy storage power plant and the largest lead-carbon battery storage facility. It was presented as a demonstration of grid flexibility, peak shaving and electricity cost reduction using domestically manufactured lead-carbon batteries. Chinese battery manufacturer Tianneng supplied the lead-carbon batteries and previously highlighted the project as a flagship application of its technology. Tianneng is not named as a defendant in the current lawsuit. In a supplementary statement dated November 18, Gisway said its subsidiary Hongsheng was responsible only for AC-side electrical design, not battery selection or DC-side engineering. The company argued that battery degradation could result from manufacturing defects, operational management or both, and said the causes and contractual responsibility remain unproven. The dispute could intensify scrutiny of lead-carbon batteries, already a marginal technology in China’s grid-scale storage market. Lithium-ion batteries accounted for 96.1% of the country’s operational new-type storage capacity at the end of 2025, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA). China’s 2022 storage development plan included lead-carbon batteries among technologies eligible for research and development. However, the government’s latest five-year implementation plan, released in November 2026, prioritizes lithium-ion improvements, sodium-ion deployment and commercialization of technologies such as compressed-air and flow batteries, without specifically identifying lead-carbon storage as a priority. For a technology seeking wider commercial acceptance, a major performance dispute involving a flagship demonstration project could further undermine investor confidence. The court’s findings on battery condition, operating practices and contractual responsibility will be important in determining the case’s wider implications. title: ZE Energy acquires 472 MWh shovel-ready BESS in Italy - Energy Storage
content: ZE Energy, a French specialist in solar energy and storage , has acquired its third battery storage project in Italy. This is the Magliano Alpi BESS project in the Piedmont region, previously developed by ReFeel New Energy, an Italian renewable energy developer backed by Gresham House Europe (formerly SUSI Partners). Fully authorized and ready for construction, this 59 MW project will have a storage capacity of nearly 480 MWh, providing up to eight hours of autonomy. Connected to the 132 kV high-voltage network via an existing Terna substation, it will bring long-term flexibility to the northern Italian network, capable of absorbing electricity when production is abundant and releasing it during periods of high demand or system tension. In an Italian electricity system where demand is projected to exceed 300 TWh in 2025, with 15% covered by net imports, the accelerated deployment of renewable energy reinforces the need to connect flexibility systems to the grid. With over 44 TWh produced in 2025, a 25% year-on-year increase, photovoltaics exemplifies this dynamic: battery storage allows for the absorption of excess energy during peak production periods, and then its return to the grid when production is insufficient to meet demand. This is why the French operator, which aims to reach 1.5 GW of installed capacity worldwide by 2030, is rapidly expanding in this market through acquisitions. The first two involved the BESS plant in Sessa Aurunca (98.5 MW/832 MWh, in the Puglia region) and the Elena plant (200 MW/1.2 GWh), also in Puglia.
